items.descriptionOriginal: "Bhandiwala, bhandiwala." For years, the familiar call was part of how 35-year-old Anil Datanini earned a living. Like other bhandiwalas , he collected old clothes , traditionally exchanged for utensils, and sold what could be reused. He had entered the trade at around 15, following work his family knew well. After moving from Gujarat to Mumbai, he continued sorting textiles and finding buyers for them. But there was one thing he could never count on: how much material he would find. Some days brought plenty of clothes; on others, hours spent looking for them yielded very little. That began to change in January 2026, when Anil partnered with Textile Waste Innovation Network (TWIN), a Mumbai-based enterprise founded by 29-year-old Vikram Shahi. Instead of sourcing everything himself, Anil now receives a more regular supply of used clothes, which he sorts, prepares and sells through markets in villages and rural areas. "Now the material comes to us regularly, so we can work properly," he says. "We sort it according to the quality and condition and then send the reusable clothes to villages." Anil says he currently earns between Rs 25,000 and Rs 30,000 a month, sometimes more. For him, the greater relief is being able to plan household expenses and save with more confidence. His experience captures an important part of TWIN's approach. According to its founder, the network has collected around 17,500 kg of used textiles and reached more than 650 households. It is doing so by working with waghari workers and bhandiwalas , whose experience in collecting and reselling clothes has long kept usable fabric in circulation. From his mother's cupboard to Mumbai's beaches When Vikram was growing up in Mumbai, he watched his mother exchange old clothes for steel utensils with a bhandiwala . He understood the exchange, but wondered what happened to those clothes afterwards. Even where recycling or upcycling options existed, there was no obvious route connecting a household's unwanted textiles to the people who could process them. Born in Bihar, with family roots in Sitamarhi, Vikram moved to Mumbai with his parents when he was three. In 2017, while studying information technology at Mumbai University, he began volunteering at clean-up drives. At Versova beach that monsoon, he noticed clothes mixed in with the plastic waste. He saw more discarded textiles during subsequent clean-ups, including around festivals such as Holi. In 2019, he began organising drives of his own with support from Bhumi NGO. The question from his childhood returned: where did damaged clothes go when they were no longer useful to their owners? In 2022, Vikram enrolled for a master's in social work at the College of Social Work, Nirmala Niketan, Mumbai. A term paper on waste management helped him explore what happens to post-consumer textiles, meaning clothes and other fabrics discarded after use. "Post-consumer textile waste was not getting the kind of attention I felt it deserved," he tells The Better India . The gap became clearer in 2024, when he joined ReCircle as a sales executive. He had initially applied to work in plastic waste management, but was offered a role involving textiles instead. "At that point, I did not know much about textile waste, but once I started working on it, I realised there was a huge gap in the collection system," he says. People had familiar ways of passing on clothes that were still wearable: donating them, giving them to relatives or exchanging them for utensils. Torn T-shirts, worn-out bedsheets and other unusable fabric were more difficult to deal with. Even where recycling or upcycling options existed, there was no obvious route connecting a household's unwanted textiles to the people who could process them. A 1,200-kg experiment in the Mumbai monsoon In August 2025, while working full time on education initiatives, including STEM labs in schools, Vikram and a few friends organised a textile collection drive in Vasai. They gathered around 1,200 kg of material, despite heavy monsoon rain complicating the collection. Vikram continued his job until February 2026, when he began focusing on the enterprise full time. "I was still working at the time, so we were doing this mostly on weekends," he recalls. "The first drive itself gave us confidence that people actually had this problem and were looking for a solution." TWIN was formally registered on 30 October 2025. Vikram continued his job until February 2026, when he began focusing on the enterprise full time. He wanted to make textile collection easier for households while giving existing recovery workers a more dependable source of material. "We are not trying to replace the existing recovery network. We are trying to build on it and create a more organised collection layer around it," he explains. What happens to clothes after TWIN collects them? TWIN collects used textiles from households, housing societies, schools, colleges, hotels, companies, NGOs and other bulk generators across the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. Household pickups are described by the enterprise as free. A resident can request a collection through TWIN's website or WhatsApp chatbot, sharing their name, location and details of the textiles. The team records the request, including the quantity and type of material, in a customer relationship management system (CRM) before verifying it and assigning a collection partner. The enterprise works with waghari and bhandiwala workers, providing training, checking backgrounds and assigning collection areas by PIN code. This helps coordinate pickups that were previously handled more informally. The collected clothes are then sorted by condition, fabric and possible next use. That step determines whether a shirt can be worn again or whether a damaged bedsheet might be more useful as raw material for another product. He wanted to make textile collection easier for households while giving existing recovery workers a more dependable source of material. "Sorting is one of the most important parts because every textile cannot go to the same place," Vikram says. "We look at the condition, quality and what the next best use can be." Wearable clothes are prioritised for reuse. Workers sell them through their existing networks in villages and second-hand markets, where buyers, including farmers, can find affordable clothing. A smaller share goes to communities through NGO partners. Fabric unsuitable for wearing can take a different route. TWIN sends suitable material to upcycling partners, including The Kapda Project and artisan groups, to be made into bags, pouches and bottle holders. It also helps connect these products with buyers, including through organisations such as Sparkling Wings and Prayas Foundation. Lower-grade textiles may be downcycled into mats, rags or wiping cloths for industrial use. Recycling remains at the pilot stage, with TWIN and its partners testing which materials can be processed further. The network therefore offers several recovery routes, rather than claiming that every collected item becomes a new garment or recycled fibre. For residents, the idea is straightforward: clothes that have outlived their original use need different destinations. TWIN says it accepts wearable and torn clothes, bedsheets and curtains, but not wet or soiled material. That distinction matters when someone is clearing out a cupboard and wondering what can actually be collected. 'Now we get clothes regularly, so there is more work' TWIN currently works with around 15 to 20 informal textile recovery workers, of whom seven to 10 are connected to a more regular supply. Some receive around 200 to 300 kg of sorted textiles from the warehouse in a week, while others collect material directly from households. TWIN currently works with around 15 to 20 informal textile recovery workers, of whom seven to 10 are connected to a more regular supply. Anil, who has lived in the Sion-Dharavi area, says this has changed how he organises his work. Earlier, much of his time went into finding textiles before he could begin sorting and selling them. Now he can spend more of it preparing clothes for buyers. "We had to go and search for clothes ourselves," he says. "Sometimes we would get material and sometimes we would not. The supply was not regular." For 22-year-old Bhavesh Dattani, the difference feels familiar. He grew up in Dharavi, where his family continued a clothes-trading livelihood after his grandparents moved from Gujarat. Before joining TWIN in December 2025, he went from neighbourhood to neighbourhood exchanging utensils for clothes. "The barter system takes a lot of time. We have to go from place to place and ask people for clothes, and we do not know how much we will collect," he says. Now, he receives reusable garments from the team. "Now we get clothes regularly, so there is more work and the income is also more regular," he adds. He does not specify his earnings, but says having material available more consistently has improved his working routine. Another worker, Vikram Shankar Chekhaliya, about 45, comes from a family in Gujarat that has worked with textiles for generations. Associated with the initiative since its early stages in July 2025, he had previously sourced, sorted and sold clothes independently, including lower-value fabric used for wiping. "Sometimes we would get good clothes, and sometimes there would be very little material. Now there is a regular supply, so it becomes easier to plan the work," he says. These workers already know how to assess clothing and where it can be sold. What TWIN is trying to add is a more predictable connection between the households discarding textiles and the markets that can use them. Who earns what when an old shirt is sold again? Although household pickups are free, the enterprise earns through the sale and recovery of collected material, as well as service-based work with organisations. Upcycled products made by partner artisans create another income stream when they are purchased by organisations or corporate clients. Reusable clothes move through existing traders and markets, allowing workers to earn from their sale. TWIN also generates revenue from recovered textiles. Upcycled products made by partner artisans create another income stream when they are purchased by organisations or corporate clients. Lower-grade materials can be sold for uses such as industrial wiping, while business-to-business services add to the model. "The idea is not just to collect waste and then store it," Vikram says. "There has to be a value chain after collection. We need to make sure the material moves to the right person or the right organisation and that there is a revenue stream to sustain the system." Vikram began with his own resources. TWIN has also received support from Mumbai Ekatra, a citizen-focused grant programme, particularly for its upcycling work. According to Vikram, the enterprise has generated about Rs 3 lakh in business revenue, with another Rs 3 lakh worth of potential business in the pipeline. It has yet to turn profitable, he says, with much of its income being put back into building the collection and sorting network. 17,500 kg of clothes collected. What comes next? The WhatsApp chatbot, launched in June 2026 after TWIN initially relied on Instagram and a Google Form, has made it easier to organise incoming requests. Vikram says it recorded more than 300 registrations in its first month. The team can also track where clothes are coming from, how much is collected and which partner should handle each pickup. Technology helps manage the movement of textiles, but the recovery itself still depends on people who know how to sort, repair, reuse or sell them. For now, the work is focused on Mumbai. Vikram hopes to expand to other cities, adapting the collection network to the workers, markets and waste patterns already present in each place. There are challenges ahead. Recycling is still being tested , the enterprise is not profitable and only part of its worker network currently receives a regular supply. The team can track where clothes are coming from, how much is collected and which partner should handle each pickup. But the model has begun to connect two needs that often sit apart: households looking for a responsible way to part with old textiles, and workers looking for material they can earn from. For Anil, that connection has a practical meaning. He still sorts clothes, finds buyers and does the work he has known since his teens. What has changed is the amount of time he needs to spend searching for the next batch, and the confidence that there will be work to return to. All pictures courtesy Vikram Shahi.

items.titleOriginal: “I Heard a Barnacle”: How Paying Attention to Nature’s Background Noise Can Reveal Animal Secrets

Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Κατά τη διάρκεια τεσσάρων ημερών στην Ολυμπιακή Χερσόνησο της Ουάσιγκτον, είδα έναν Ολυμπιακό…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Phil Starks , an associate professor of biology at Tufts University, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . During four days on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula, I saw an Olympic marmot , a species found nowhere else on Earth; four bumblebee species working the same lavender plant; three western hermit crab species new to me; and five orcas slicing through the dark water off Ediz Hook . Any one of them could have been the trip’s highlight. Yet the encounter I cannot stop talking about occurred at low tide at Tongue Point , when I heard a barnacle. While I had seen thousands of barnacles, I had never imagined I could hear one. It made a noise that sounded like: Clickety-clack. Clickety-clack. Pop. As a professor who teaches about animal behavior , I know that the distinction between encountering an animal and actually noticing what it is doing is one of the simplest ways into natural history . It requires no laboratory and, at first, no special expertise. Mostly it requires learning how to let something ordinary become interesting again. At Low Tide My habit in places like a rocky shore is to become still and let my vision soften. Instead of staring at one point, I allow movement anywhere in the visual field to pull my attention. At Tongue Point, I was thinking about the demands of life in the intertidal zone , the shore between high and low tide: temperature swings, desiccation, and the cost of remaining clamped shut in open air. Then I noticed the soundscape. At first, the clicking was just coastal noise. I attributed it to small shore crabs moving among the mussels, or hermit crab shells knocking against them. Then one sharp pop pulled my attention to a single acorn barnacle . Its tiny opening was slightly unsealed, and two small plates were moving against its deeply ridged shell. The movement appeared to coincide with another pop. Then another. The repetition gave me something to follow. You can train yourself to do this almost anywhere. Watch honeybees fly around and see what you notice. When I take students or my sons to watch honeybees , I tell them not to stare directly at the hive entrance. Instead, sit nearby, look toward the open sky, and relax your gaze. At first you see empty air. Then a bee crosses it. Then another. Within moments the emptiness becomes a busy airport of arrivals and departures. Nothing new has entered the scene. You have just changed what you are capable of noticing. A Web of Assumptions Observation has its own traps. Sometimes you can miss behavior because it blends into the background. Other times you see something perfectly but stop asking questions because somebody has already told you what it means. Orb-weaver spiders offer a good example . Some add conspicuous bands or patches of dense silk to their webs. These structures are called stabilimenta , a name inherited from the old idea that they stabilize or strengthen the web. But they don’t. Researchers later found evidence for several possible functions: attracting prey, deterring or confusing predators, protecting webs from larger animals, and, in some cases, helping with temperature regulation. Different functions may matter in different species, environments, or stages of life. Muhammad Mahdi Karim/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA This orb-weaver rests on the stabilimentum of its web. I first became interested in the debate over stabilimentum function because I was unconvinced that one explanation could account for all the evidence. I started out asking whether somebody was wrong. The better question turned out to be why researchers expected one universal answer in the first place. That remains one of my favorite lessons from animal behavior: A name can be useful, but it can also sneak in an explanation. Once you think you know what something is, you become less likely to watch what it actually does. Seeing Isn’t Knowing The opposite mistake is just as easy: seeing something interesting and immediately deciding you understand it. After I returned from the Olympic Peninsula, I emailed a retired marine invertebrate zoologist and described what I had seen and heard. His response was delighted and appropriately skeptical: “Doubt it. Take a short video next time.” Aleria Jensen/NOAA/NMFS/AKFSC via Flickr How would you confirm these barnacles made a sound? I saw an open barnacle move and heard a pop at the same time. That is an observation. I did not demonstrate that the barnacle produced the sound. A mussel bed contains crabs, moving shells, and a host of other possible sources. A close-up video with synchronized audio could test whether the same visible movement repeatedly coincided with each pop. Noticing something is the start of science. It does not let you skip the work that follows. Look Again For anyone who wants to become a better naturalist , a simple sequence helps: Notice something. Describe it carefully. Ask what else could explain it. Decide what evidence would distinguish among those possibilities. Try it somewhere familiar: a backyard, city park, pond edge, patch of flowers, or shoreline. Stay longer than feels necessary. Let the sights and sounds become background. Then look for repetition. One movement, then another like it. One sound that separates from the rest. An animal returning to the same place. And once something catches your attention, resist the urge to explain it too quickly. Watch again. You may discover something genuinely unusual. More likely, you will discover something ordinary that you had never actually seen before. I may not have witnessed rare behavior at Tongue Point or identified a rare species. But I stayed long enough to wonder what I was hearing. Maybe that was rare enough. RELATED: What Are the Mysterious Creatures Quacking Under the Sea? We’re a Step Closer to Finding Out

items.titleOriginal: Fall hunger is real: four reasons your appetite changes with the season
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Ίσως έχετε προσέξει να επικρατεί τις τελευταίες εβδομάδες. Τελειώνετε το μεσημεριανό γεύμα και μια ώρα αργότερα πηγαίνετε ήδη πίσω προς την κουζίνα. Το μπολ με τη σούπα που θα σε είχε χορτάσει τον Μάιο μόλις και μετά βίας κάνει ένα βαθούλωμα, και κάπου γύρω στις τέσσερις θα ανταλλάξεις σχεδόν τα πάντα με μια ζεστή φέτα κάτι…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Maybe you’ve noticed it creeping in over the last few weeks. You finish lunch, and an hour later you’re already drifting back toward the kitchen. The bowl of soup that would have filled you up in May barely makes a dent, and somewhere around four o’clock you’d trade almost anything for a warm slice of something with cinnamon on top. It’s easy to blame the pumpkin bread and cider doughnuts suddenly everywhere you look, and they’re certainly not helping. But if you’ve been feeling hungrier in the fall, there’s more going on than seasonal temptation. Your body is responding to shorter days, colder air, and some very old instincts, all at the same time. Registered dietitian Lyndsay Hall of JM Nutrition walked through what’s behind that bigger appetite, and the good news is that none of it means you’re doing anything wrong. Why you feel hungrier in the fall Old instincts that haven’t caught up For most of human history, the end of summer meant leaner months were coming. “For those living in colder climates, fall signifies the transition from summer to winter, when historically food access would have been limited in the coming months, so people would eat more and put on some extra weight intentionally to help them get through the cold winter season,” Hall said. Your grocery store stays stocked all year, of course, but your body doesn’t know that. Like animals building up reserves before hibernation, some of that seasonal pull toward eating more may be wiring we’ve carried with us for a very long time. Staying warm takes energy Cold weather asks more of you physically, too. “When we start to feel physically cold, our bodies will expend more energy trying to keep us warm (i.e., by shivering) and diverting more blood flow to organs to keep them up and running,” Hall said. More energy spent means your body sends stronger signals to refuel. Less sunlight, shifting moods Then there’s the light, or the lack of it. “Many people experience a drop in serotonin levels during the fall and winter months due to decreased sun exposure and the cold weather making it difficult to get outside as often as we might during the summer months,” Hall said. Lower serotonin can affect hunger and fullness cues, making cravings stronger and meals feel less satisfying. For some people, the darker months bring more than a mild case of the winter blues . If low mood, fatigue, or changes in appetite start to feel heavy or stick around, it’s a good idea to check in with a doctor, since seasonal affective disorder is common and very treatable. Holidays on the horizon Fall also kicks off the stretch of the year when so many gatherings revolve around food. “Over time, we have created psychological associations between certain times of year and eating more or indulging. Thanksgiving, for example, occurs in the fall months and is often centered around eating that many look forward to,” Hall said. The same goes for Christmas, Hanukkah, Kwanzaa and New Year’s, when the dishes on the table tend to be rich, hearty and tied up with memories. Staying satisfied through fall and winter None of this calls for a diet or a calorie tracker. Hall’s approach is to lean on three things that help meals stick with you longer: protein, fiber, and healthy fats. “Protein and fiber help to keep us physically satiated for longer periods of time,” she said. Together with fats, they slow digestion, so a cozy meal keeps you going well into the afternoon. Fold protein into the comfort foods you love Hall suggests stirring Greek yogurt or cottage cheese, or a high-protein plant-based alternative, into muffin batter, pancakes, and quick breads. A splash of milk or a dairy-free version in your oatmeal or morning latte works the same way. Eggs, tofu, fish and poultry can round out casseroles and pasta bakes, too. Let vegetables and legumes do the heavy lifting Soups, stews and chilis are perfect for this. Skin-on potatoes, winter squash, eggplant, peppers, leafy greens and green beans add fiber without changing the spirit of a dish, and apples or pomegranate seeds bring a bright, seasonal crunch to salads. “Beans, chickpeas and lentils are great ways to add both protein and lots of fiber to soups, stews, chilis and stuffed vegetables,” Hall said. Give seasonal baking a fiber boost Seasonal treats can pull a little more weight, too. “Oat bran, chia, ground flaxseed, grated zucchini or carrot, and dried fruits can be easy sources of extra fiber for any baked good or hot cereals,” Hall said. So the next time your stomach rumbles an hour after lunch on a gray November afternoon, you can take it as your body doing what it’s long been built to do. Answer it with something warm and filling, save room for the dishes that only come around once a year, and let the season be one you enjoy at the table instead of second-guessing every bite. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A once-daily tablet called AR1001 slowed cognitive decline by 31 percent over a year in people with early Alzheimer’s disease who were not on any other Alzheimer’s medication, according to phase 3 results presented at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference in Boston. The Alzheimer’s pill, developed by South Korean company AriBio, belongs to the same drug family as Viagra. Across the full trial population, which included patients already taking other Alzheimer’s drugs, the effect did not reach statistical significance. How the Alzheimer’s pill works A PDE5 inhibitor, not an amyloid drug AR1001 is a phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE5) inhibitor. Drugs in this class relax blood vessels, which is how they work for erectile dysfunction, and for the brain the effect is increased blood flow. Tara Spires-Jones, a professor of neurodegeneration at the University of Edinburgh and a fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences, said the mechanism likely goes beyond circulation. “This drug acts through boosting blood flow and likely also directly stimulating pathways in brain cells that promote learning and memory ,” she said. That sets it apart from the disease-modifying treatments that have come through late-stage trials in recent years, which target amyloid, the protein that builds up into plaques in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s. Dr. Sheona Scales, director of research at Alzheimer’s Research UK , called AR1001 “especially interesting” for that reason. “Rather than targeting amyloid, it acts on a specific enzyme and influences several other processes involved in brain function ,” she said. A tablet instead of an infusion The format matters too. Existing disease-modifying options require infusions or injections, while AR1001 is swallowed once a day. Dr. Richard Oakley, associate director of research and innovation at Alzheimer’s Society, said that difference “could make treatment simpler.” Phase 3 trial results in detail 13 countries, 604 key participants The phase 3 trial, known as Polaris-AD , enrolled patients with early Alzheimer’s across 13 countries, including the UK. The headline result comes from the 604 participants who were taking no other Alzheimer’s drugs, a group in which the decline in memory and thinking slowed by nearly a third compared with placebo. “Over the year of the trial, this drug was able to effectively slow down people’s decline in memory and thinking by nearly a third, and the side-effects reported were mostly mild to moderate,” Oakley said. The subgroup question The catch is in the wider group. Among patients who were also taking existing medications for Alzheimer’s symptoms, AR1001 did not produce a statistically significant benefit, which means the trial missed significance across its full population. Scales acknowledged as much. “The trial demonstrated a statistically significant slowing of clinical decline in participants who were not taking other commonly used Alzheimer’s medications alongside the trial drug. However, this benefit was not significant across the overall trial group,” she said. Oakley said the reason for that gap needs further investigation. Next steps for a new Alzheimer’s treatment Regulators and further trials None of the experts treated the results as final. All called for additional trials, and the findings still need review by independent scientists and drug regulators before AR1001 could be prescribed. Oakley also warned against improvising with existing drugs. “AR1001 is from the same family of medicines as Viagra, but it is being developed specifically for Alzheimer’s disease,” he said, adding that people should not take Viagra to try to treat the condition. A different route against dementia The stakes are large. Alzheimer’ s is the most common form of dementia, and dementia is forecast to affect 153 million people worldwide by 2050, with no cure available. Scales described the results as “an important milestone in the search for new Alzheimer’s treatments,” and Oakley said they were “an exciting sign that we could have a totally new treatment for early Alzheimer’s disease that tackles its causes, not just its symptoms.” If larger studies confirm the effect and explain why it disappeared in patients on other medications, a daily tablet working through blood flow would give doctors a second line of attack alongside the amyloid drugs. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Could Smarter Energy Habits Make Outdoor Living More Sustainable? Reading Time: 2 minutes Could Smarter Energy Habits Make Outdoor Living More Sustainable? Picture a weekend camping trip where your devices stay charged, your food stays fresh, and you have everything you need to enjoy a comfortable escape, all without using more energy than necessary. It might sound like a balancing act, but sustainable outdoor living is becoming easier thanks to smarter technology and a few simple changes in how we use energy. Whether you love camping, traveling in an RV, or entertaining in your backyard, your energy habits can have a bigger environmental impact than you might realize. Fortunately, reducing that impact doesn’t have to mean giving up the little comforts that make spending time outdoors so enjoyable. Make Better Use Of Natural Resources Nature already provides some of the resources you need to enjoy outdoor living comfortably. Making the most of natural daylight, for example, can significantly reduce your reliance on artificial lighting. Try planning outdoor activities around daylight hours and positioning your campsite or seating area to maximize natural light. When evening arrives, solar-powered lanterns and energy-efficient LED lights can provide illumination without consuming large amounts of electricity. Solar technology has also made it easier to generate electricity in remote locations, allowing you to enjoy modern conveniences while reducing your dependence on traditional power sources. Choose Smarter Ways To Power Your Adventures Keeping your essential equipment running is often one of the biggest challenges of spending extended periods outdoors. From charging smartphones to powering portable refrigerators, reliable electricity can make your adventures much more comfortable. However, not every activity requires a large generator or constant access to mains electricity. Portable power stations, rechargeable batteries, and solar-compatible equipment can offer practical alternatives. Looking at the equipment available from Power and Pedal can help you find power solutions suited to different outdoor activities . Choosing equipment that matches your energy requirements can reduce unnecessary consumption while ensuring you have sufficient power when you need it. Think Carefully About Your Outdoor Equipment It’s easy to accumulate gadgets and appliances when you enjoy outdoor activities, but not everything needs to be powered by electricity. For example, a well-insulated cooler might be sufficient for a weekend trip, eliminating the need for an electric refrigerator. Similarly, investing in quality thermal clothing and blankets can help you stay comfortable during cooler evenings without relying heavily on electric heating. When electrical equipment is necessary, prioritize energy-efficient models and maintain them properly to extend their lifespan. Plan Ahead To Avoid Wasting Energy Good preparation is one of the simplest ways to improve your outdoor energy habits. Charging devices before leaving home, downloading entertainment for offline use, and checking equipment before traveling can reduce unnecessary power consumption. Planning meals carefully can also help. Preparing ingredients in advance and choosing dishes that require less cooking time can reduce fuel use, especially on longer camping trips. Make Sustainability Part Of Your Outdoor Lifestyle Creating a more sustainable outdoor lifestyle doesn’t require dramatic changes. Often, it’s the smaller decisions that make the greatest difference when repeated consistently. By making thoughtful equipment choices, using renewable energy where practical, and avoiding unnecessary waste, you can reduce your environmental footprint without compromising your enjoyment. The goal isn’t to eliminate energy use entirely. It’s to use the energy you need more efficiently, allowing you to enjoy comfortable outdoor adventures while taking better care of the natural spaces you love exploring. The post Could Smarter Energy Habits Make Outdoor Living More Sustainable? appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Data from 10,000 workers show sit-stand desks boost active work time by 43 minutes a day—or roughly $9,000 in annual productivity per employee. Every workday is a negotiation between our bodies and our jobs. Sit too long, our backs and necks protest; stand too long, our feet might have something to say about it. Sit-stand desks, also known as height-adjustable desks or standing desks, promise a healthier way to work, giving employees the flexibility to alternate between sitting and standing throughout the day. Now, new research suggests these desks may be giving employees, and employers, another benefit beyond ergonomics and well-being: productivity. Drawing on data from more than 10,000 employees, researchers at Texas A&M University found that workers who used sit-stand desks averaged 43 additional minutes of active computer use each day compared with those using regular desks, a difference that could translate to nearly $9,000 in annual productivity per employee. The study, published in Theoretical and Applied Ergonomics , was co-led by Texas A&M School of Public Health professor Mark Benden and US Army Public Health Command Region, West, Regional Ergonomist Tricia Salzar. The findings suggest that the physical workspace may be a powerful, often overlooked, influence on employee well-being, productivity, and even a company’s overall performance. When organizations look to boost performance and productivity, they turn to new technologies, training programs and management strategies. But another powerful influence may be hiding in plain sight: the physical workplace itself. “It’s what we call the ‘workplace effect,'” Benden says. “The direct impact that the physical work environment has on the behavior, health, psychological well-being, and even engagement and performance of employees.” Sit-stand desks are a striking example of the workplace effect. Rather than locking employees into a single position for hours at a time, they give workers the flexibility to sit, stand and move throughout the day, as tasks and energy levels shift. “It can have a profound effect,” Benden says. “Alternating between different working positions promotes better health outcomes by reducing physical strain and encouraging movement for those who might otherwise spend most of their workday sedentary.” But the benefits may extend beyond physical health. Benden and Salzar’s new research shows that sit-stand desks can also have a substantial impact on productivity. “It has a cumulative, positive effect for both employers and employees,” Benden says. For employees, height-adjustable desks could lead to sustained energy and longer stretches of focused work. For employers, the higher work productivity could translate into a nearly $9,000 return on investment per employee annually. “The implications are hard to ignore,” Benden says. “When we design workplaces around employees and their needs, better health, better performance and better organizational outcomes follow.” The takeaway? Investing in the physical workplace, like height-adjustable desks, isn’t just good for employee comfort and health; it could be good for business, too. To test whether sit-stand desks could influence work output and productivity, Benden and his colleagues stepped out of their labs and turned to the real world, using a resource few ergonomics studies can match. “We analyzed a huge dataset of more than 10,000 workers over a yearlong period, comparing the total computer use of traditional desk users and height-adjustable desk users,” Benden says. The records paired employee comfort surveys with a digital trail of workplace activity, tracking everything from keystrokes and words typed to mouse clicks and typing errors, all to paint a detailed picture of how employees interacted with their computers throughout the workday. “It was important that we collected subjective measurements, like employee survey responses of their comfort and objective measurements of computer activity through software, to analyze how people engaged with their work,” Benden says. The team found that workers with sit-stand desks averaged 3.66 hours of active computer time, compared with 2.95 hours among regular-desk employees—a gap of about 43 minutes a day. That might not sound like much, but over a year it adds up to roughly 171 additional hours, or more than four 40-hour workweeks. And those additional hours come with a practical price tag, too. Multiplying the 171 additional hours by a standardized hourly wage of about $52, the researchers estimate that sit-stand desks could generate nearly $9,000 in potential annual productivity value per employee. “Our findings were exciting because they suggest that height-adjustable desks can directly influence overall work output and economic organizational productivity,” Benden says. The researchers also found that employees using sit-stand desks generally typed more words and logged more keystrokes than their counterparts at non-adjustable desks. “The data showed that people aren’t just engaging with their work, they are producing output in a meaningful way,” Benden says. For Benden, the findings open the door to broader questions about the future of organizations, focusing on another force rapidly reshaping the modern workplace. “Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly integrated into daily work,” Benden says. “Just as we’ve studied how the physical environment affects human health and performance, we’re interested in understanding how emerging AI technologies could influence the physical workspace and outcomes of organizations.” From adjustable desks to emerging technologies, the underlying question remains the same: how can organizations design environments and systems to better support the people who use them? “The next breakthrough may not come from working harder, but from designing workspaces and systems that help people work smarter and more efficiently,” Benden says. The story told by the more than 10,000 employees is that the desk may be doing far more than just holding up your computer. For Benden, sit-stand desks represent more than an ergonomic innovation. They’re part of a lifelong passion to understand how workplaces can be designed to better support employee well-being and organizational success. “We spend a lot of time at work,” Benden says. “It’s my passion to make sure that workers feel supported in their workplace, built on informed and guided scientific evidence.” A former Army Reserve officer, engineer, healthcare professional, inventor and world-renowned researcher, Benden has spent decades studying the complex relationship between people and the environments in which they work. So, the next time you find yourself slumping in your chair at 3pm with an aching back, don’t just reach for another cup of coffee, because the verdict is in: show this study to your boss. Your back—and your company’s bottom line—will thank you. Source: Texas A&M University The post Sit-stand desks boost active work time by 43 minutes a day appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: #thebetterindia **184 trees face the axe in Mumbai. Thousands have objected. But is anyone listening?** 🌳 In Mumbai's Versova, residents once transformed a garbage dump into Nana Nani Park, reclaiming a neglected space and turning it into a green haven for the community. Today, that same park faces an uncertain future, with the proposed felling of **184 trees despite thousands of objections**. At a time when Mumbai is debating the future of its urban green spaces, Bhutan offers a powerful example of what sustainable development can look like. Recognised at the Earthshot Prize ceremony in Mumbai, Bhutan has made environmental conservation central to its vision of progress. Its Constitution mandates that **at least 60% of the country's land remain under forest cover**, reflecting a commitment to protecting nature for future generations. 🌿 The contrast raises an important question: **Can urban development truly be called progress if it comes at the cost of the environment?** As Mumbai continues to expand, the debate surrounding Nana Nani Park highlights a larger challenge facing Indian cities: balancing infrastructure development with environmental protection, climate resilience and public well-being. Urban parks and green spaces are not luxuries. They are essential to cleaner air, healthier communities, biodiversity and a better quality of life. A city can build taller skyscrapers and bigger infrastructure projects, but if its residents lose access to nature, what kind of future is it really creating? **Mumbai's 184 trees are more than just a local environmental issue. They represent a larger conversation about sustainable cities, urban development and the true meaning of progress.** What should come first: rapid urban development or protecting the green spaces that make our cities liveable? **Tell us what you think in the comments.** 🌱 #NanaNaniPark #SaveMumbaiTrees #MumbaiNews #Versova #SaveTrees #Bhutan #EarthshotPrize #SustainableDevelopment #ClimateAction #UrbanGreenSpaces #EnvironmentalConservation #MumbaiEnvironment #GreenCities #ClimateChange #thebetterindia [Mumbai Nana Nani Park, Nana Nani Park Versova, 184 trees Mumbai, Mumbai tree cutting controversy, save Mumbai trees, Versova Nana Nani Park, Mumbai environmental news, Bhutan Earthshot Prize, Earthshot Prize 2026, Bhutan forest conservation, Bhutan 60 percent forest cover, sustainable urban development India, Mumbai green spaces, urban deforestation India, environmental conservation India, climate action India, Mumbai development projects, save trees Mumbai, sustainable cities India, urban green spaces importance, The Better India] “Episode” licensed via Music Vine: FWECZ62E8KJQL3BZ Subscribe Us Now : https://www.youtube.com/thebetterindia Follow us for more: Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/thebetterindia Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/thebetterindia/ Twitter: https://twitter.com/thebetterindia LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/thebetterindia/ Website: https://www.thebetterindia.com/

items.descriptionOriginal: On the night of 26 November 2008, Mumbai Police officer Sanjay Govilkar was shot while helping capture terrorist Ajmal Kasab at Girgaum Chowpatty. Across Mumbai, terrorists were attacking several locations. People across India followed the news from their homes, fearful of what might happen next. Police officers responded across the city, and many lost their lives in the process. Sanjay survived the bullet injury. Years later, he continues to speak about that night, the colleagues he lost, and the work that has filled his life beyond the police force. From writing books to helping families through an NGO he founded with friends, he has found different ways to serve people. The Better India spoke to the former officer about the arrest of Kasab and the experiences that shaped his life afterwards. 'Unfortunately, he never returned' "I consider myself very lucky, as the bullet Kasab fired at me hit the left-hand side of my abdomen and not the right," he smiles. Around the time of the attacks, Sanjay had been excited about the release of his book, Stopwatch . He was going around his colleagues' desks to distribute copies to everyone. Shortly before the attacks began in Mumbai, he visited his boss Hemant Karkare's cabin to give him a copy. "Hemant sir was not there for some reason, so I left a copy for him on his desk. Unfortunately, he never returned," Sanjay recalls. The night he helped capture Kasab alive "As the attack unfolded, we were tense, but we had only one goal: to serve our nation. The moment I heard that my boss, Hemant sir, had been attacked and lost his life, I was upset," he shares. Later that night, Sanjay and his fellow police officers confronted Kasab at Girgaum Chowpatty. During the encounter, Sanjay was shot. "My colleague wanted to immediately shoot him down, but I convinced him to arrest him, as he was a key witness," Sanjay shares. Capturing Kasab alive became an important part of the investigation and trial that followed. Sanjay and his fellow police officers confronted Kasab at Girgaum Chowpatty. During the encounter, Sanjay was shot. "After the arrest, I was immediately rushed to the hospital, where I received treatment for five to six days. I was asked to stay away from the news and was given counselling by a group of doctors. Finally, when I was discharged, I saw that all the noise was settling. My doctors and my family took great care of me," he smiles. The experience left Sanjay with a sense of pride in his service, though he is careful to share the credit with his colleagues. When asked how it feels to have achieved something so significant, he says, "I am extremely proud of serving my country, and I would never want to take advantage of this." He goes on to credit his entire team for the recognition. Why a police officer began writing about health While Sanjay says that being a cop and serving the country was his duty, he was always driven by another passion away from work: writing. Sanjay has so far written and published five books, all of them on health, mental health and relationships. One of those was Stopwatch , the book he had just published when the 26/11 attacks took place. "At one point in my career, I was posted as an immigration officer at the airport and had erratic shifts. This took a toll on my health and prompted me to write the book Stopwatch . It is a must-read for all people who work night shifts," he shares. "I never let my professional experiences shape my writing. I incorporate the lessons I have learnt, but never let them influence my writing," he says. Sanjay maintains clear boundaries between his profession and passion. "I never let my professional experiences shape my writing. I incorporate the lessons I have learnt, but never let them influence my writing," he says. 'My biggest asset is my close friends' His friendships have also shaped another important part of his life. Together with his close friends, Sanjay runs Jeevarang, an NGO inspired by a deeply personal experience. "Twenty-five years ago, I lost my grandmother. She was very dear to me. We cremated her in my village, and the next day, when we visited the site to collect her ashes, we saw dogs feeding on the remains. I was heartbroken by what I saw," he shares. The memory stayed with him and became one of the reasons he wanted to help families give their loved ones a dignified farewell. Through Jeevarang, Sanjay and his friends assist families who have lost their loved ones across 21 villages in Maharashtra. They provide support in cash or kind, depending on what the families need. The NGO began operations in 2007 and also encourages writers by sponsoring the publication of their books. A fraud case that inspired his next chapter Sanjay retired from the police in July 2026. But his interest in helping people facing difficult situations has continued into his retirement. He now runs his own legal and risk advisory firm. The idea goes back to a case he encountered during his police career, involving a mother and daughter who lost their livelihood to online fraud. "I came across a peculiar case in my career in 2009. Online fraudsters tricked a mother and daughter. They were told they had won a lottery and were asked to pay a huge sum of money. The women were innocent and, assuming they would receive a large amount, they sold their small pull-cart shop in Mumbai and lost all their money. The department, however, intervened and cracked the case. This incident stayed with me, and I decided that I wanted to help people who feel stuck in legal issues. That's when I came up with this idea," he shares. The mother and daughter's experience stayed with Sanjay, much like what he had witnessed after his grandmother's cremation years earlier. Both experiences influenced the work he eventually chose to pursue outside policing. When Sanjay speaks about 26/11, he credits his colleagues for what they achieved together. In the years since, he has continued to act on the concerns that have stayed with him, from helping families arrange a dignified farewell to supporting people facing legal difficulties. Individuals seeking guidance or assistance with legal matters and risk-related concerns can find information about the services offered by Govilkar Legal & Risk Advisory on its official website . The firm aims to help people understand complex legal situations and consider their next steps.

items.descriptionOriginal: You twist open a sealed bottle of water and drink without a second thought. It's clear, it's sealed, and it's been purified. Behind that bottle is more checking than most of us realise. Since November 2024, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has treated packaged drinking water as a "high-risk" food. The label doesn't mean the water is dangerous. It means the product gets stricter scrutiny: inspections before a licence is granted, annual inspections, and regular testing of both the water and its packaging. Those checks exist because some things in water can't be seen, smelt or tasted. A recent case shows why they matter. FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd after a water sample from its Goa plant was declared unsafe. The sample reportedly contained bromate at 12 micrograms per litre, above the limit of 10. A referral laboratory later also found polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, or PAHs. Bisleri disputes the findings. It says independent testing found bromate within the limit, that its water is safe, and that it will cooperate with the regulator. Whatever the outcome, the case raises a question most of us have never thought to ask: if water has been purified, how can chemicals linked to cancer end up in it? Here's what bromate and PAHs are, how they get into water, what levels are considered acceptable, and what the rules say about keeping them out. What happened at Bisleri's Goa plant? On 30 September 2025, FSSAI officials collected six samples from Bisleri's Goa facility. According to the company, five met the standards. The sixth showed bromate at 12 micrograms per litre, two above the limit. FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd after a water sample from its Goa plant was declared unsafe. Photograph: (Plastic Pollution Coalition) Bisleri says it appealed on 22 November 2025, and the sample went to a referral laboratory. That lab found bromate within the limit, but detected PAHs. Bisleri also had the same sample tested at an FSSAI-approved lab, which it says found bromate within the permitted limit. It sent those results to FSSAI's Western Regional Office on 2 February 2026 . After that, the company says, it heard nothing more and assumed the matter was closed. FSSAI, however, declared the sample unsafe and sanctioned prosecution under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. It has also said it plans to test more samples from Bisleri and other packaged water companies. A prosecution sanction is not a conviction. And because the labs reported different results, it matters to separate what each test actually found from what is still disputed. How does bromate get into water? Surprisingly, bromate often comes from the very step meant to make water safe. Many bottlers disinfect water with ozone, a powerful gas that kills bacteria and viruses. But some water sources naturally contain bromide. When ozone meets bromide during treatment, the reaction can produce bromate. The World Health Organization (WHO) says this treatment process, called ozonation , is the main reason bromate shows up in drinking water. Normally, it isn't found in water in any significant amount. How much forms depends on four things: how much bromide was in the water to begin with how much ozone is used the water's pH (how acidic or alkaline it is) how long treatment runs Get the balance wrong and levels can climb. The WHO has recorded bromate anywhere from under 2 to 293 micrograms per litre in ozone-treated water. Many bottlers disinfect water with ozone, a powerful gas that kills bacteria and viruses. Photograph: (The Hospital of Central Connecticut) Bromate can also form when chlorine-based disinfectants are produced using salt that contains bromide impurities. So bromate in water doesn't necessarily mean the source was polluted. It can be a by-product of cleaning the water, which is why the treatment process itself needs close watching. How much is too much? Bromate worries scientists because it caused cancer in laboratory animals. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies potassium bromate as Group 2B, or "possibly carcinogenic to humans". Its 1999 review found strong evidence of cancer in animals, but not enough evidence in humans. That difference matters. A chemical being a possible cancer hazard doesn't mean every exposure carries the same risk. How much is present, and for how long someone is exposed, both count. The WHO's provisional limit for bromate in drinking water is 10 micrograms per litre (0.01 milligrams per litre). India's standard for packaged drinking water, BIS IS 14543:2024, also lists bromate as a chemical that must be tested. In the Bisleri case, 12 micrograms is two above the limit. That's a regulatory concern, but it doesn't mean anyone who drank the water will develop cancer or fall ill. Judging the real risk would need three things: how concentrated it was, how much someone drank, and for how long. Two things are true at once. Detecting a chemical doesn't automatically make water unsafe, because it's the amount that counts. And staying within the limit doesn't mean manufacturers can stop checking. What are PAHs, and how do they get into water? PAHs are a large family of chemicals, built from two or more linked rings of carbon atoms. They form mainly when things don't burn completely, such as coal, wood, petrol and other organic material. Vehicle exhaust, factory emissions and other burning release them into the air and the environment. PAHs don't dissolve easily in water. Instead, they tend to cling to tiny particles. According to the WHO , one known route into drinking water is the coal-tar coating used inside older water pipes to stop them corroding. Pollution from burning can also settle on soil and water, and wash into water sources as runoff. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies potassium bromate as Group 2B, or "possibly carcinogenic to humans". Photograph: (Image generated by AI) One PAH, benzo[a]pyrene, is a particular concern because it can cause cancer. The WHO's limit for it is 0.7 micrograms per litre. But PAHs are not all alike. One compound causing cancer doesn't mean they all carry the same risk. Finding PAHs in a sample also doesn't tell us how they got there. In the Bisleri case, we would need to know which compounds were found, and in what amounts, to judge how serious the finding is or where it came from. What about the plastic bottle? Bromate comes mainly from treatment, not the bottle. But scientists have looked at whether chemicals can leach from packaging into water. A 2022 study in the Bulletin of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology tested PET bottles and low-density polyethylene water packets in India. It found that the amount of plasticisers seeping into water depended on the packaging material, how long the water was stored and how hot it got. Leaching was higher at high temperatures, especially in recycled PET bottles and plastic packets. That's a good reason to pay attention to packaging and storage. But the study looked at phthalates, not bromate or PAHs, so it doesn't show that bottles caused either contaminant discussed here. What checks are already in place? Under FSSAI's 29 November 2024 order , packaged drinking water is a high-risk food category. This means: manufacturers must be inspected before they get a licence or registration inspections happen once a year centrally licensed manufacturers need an annual third-party food safety audit by an FSSAI-recognised agency From 1 January 2026, a new FSSAI testing scheme also requires manufacturers to: test their source water at FSSAI-notified, NABL-accredited labs before using it, and test any new source before it's used test for microbes every month, and for several chemicals every quarter test every parameter in the standard at least once every six months test monthly if a parameter fails, until three batches in a row pass The packaging is covered too. Bottles, jars and caps must be tested every six months for "overall and colour migration", meaning whether material or colour seeps from the packaging into the water. Manufacturers must keep these records for inspection. How does a failed sample end up in court? The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 , sets out the steps (Sections 42, 46 and 47): A Food Safety Officer collects a sample and sends it to a Food Analyst, who usually has 14 days to report. If the manufacturer disputes the result, it can appeal to the Designated Officer, who can send the sample to a referral laboratory. If the findings show a violation serious enough to prosecute, the case goes to the relevant authority for sanction. A 2022 study in the Bulletin of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology tested PET bottles and low-density polyethylene water packets in India. Photograph: (Food & Wine) In the Bisleri case, the company challenged the first result, the sample went to a referral lab, and FSSAI then sanctioned prosecution. Bisleri's independent results and its response are part of a dispute that will now be settled through the regulatory and legal process. Should consumers be worried? Chemical contaminants can't always be detected by taste, smell or look. Clear water isn't necessarily free of chemicals . But the Bisleri findings concern one regulatory sample. They don't prove that all packaged water, or every batch from the company, is unsafe. Safe drinking water depends on consistent testing and monitoring. Purification is non-negotiable, but the chemicals that can form during treatment, and contamination from storage and pipes, deserve just as much attention.

items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative gum disease treatment that uses egg yolk antibodies and near-infrared light to destroy harmful bacteria without harming beneficial microbes. Unlike conventional treatments, the approach preserves the mouth's natural bacterial balance and protects healthy gum cells. In mice, it significantly reduced the bone loss associated with periodontitis, a major cause of tooth loss.

items.descriptionOriginal: When trees along a road are marked for felling, the loss extends beyond their shade and canopy. For thousands of orchids growing on their trunks and branches, the removal of a single tree can mean losing their entire habitat. In Kozhikode, Kerala, researchers faced this challenge as road-widening projects threatened mature trees supporting native orchids. Instead of allowing the plants to be lost along with the trees, they began rescuing and relocating them to other landscapes. A study published on 15 October 2026 in the scientific journal Plants has now documented the outcomes of this effort. Researchers assessed 27,324 native orchids belonging to 21 species that were relocated to three sites in Kozhikode. After monitoring them for 12 to 24 months, they found that 19,511, or 71.4%, had survived. Why roadside trees matter to orchids Unlike terrestrial orchids that grow in soil, epiphytic orchids grow on the trunks and branches of other plants. They use trees as support, relying on their bark, moisture, shade and surrounding canopy conditions to survive. When a mature host tree is felled, the orchids growing on it can lose their habitat at once. The scale of this dependence is evident from an earlier survey in Kerala. A 2025 study, Distribution and Abundance of Native Orchids on Roadside Trees in a Global Biodiversity Hotspot , recorded nearly 10,000 orchids belonging to 13 species on approximately 600 trees across Wayanad. The trees represented 72 different taxa, and the orchid population included six regional endemics. The October 2026 study notes that road construction and widening have increasingly threatened these mature host trees and the orchid communities they support. The researchers involved in the latest study included Mithun Venugopal and Pradeep N Sukumaran of the KSCSTE-Malabar Botanical Garden and Institute for Plant Sciences in Kozhikode, and Viswambharan Sarasan of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, in the UK. More than 17,000 native orchids representing 22 species had initially been transferred to Sarovaram Biopark as part of the earlier rescue programme. The subsequent effort also involved relocating orchids to two other sites: the Malabar Botanical Garden and Kappad Beach. Three sites, different survival outcomes The researchers examined how the rescued plants adapted to three distinct environments, all located in Kozhikode's coastal region. Sarovaram Biopark, an urban wetland with mangrove cover, provided a humid and relatively sheltered environment. The Malabar Botanical Garden offered a mix of shaded, marshy and moderately elevated areas. Unlike terrestrial orchids that grow in soil, epiphytic orchids grow on the trunks and branches of other plants. Photograph: (tspkumar via iNaturalist) Kappad Beach, meanwhile, exposed the orchids to stronger winds, direct sunlight and salt spray. The differences were reflected in their survival. According to the study, Sarovaram recorded the strongest overall establishment , while the exposed coastal location presented greater challenges for the plants to take root and survive. However, Kappad recorded the highest flowering rate among surviving orchids, at 35.6%. It also had the highest proportion of flowering plants producing capsules, at 62.3%. At Sarovaram, the corresponding figures were 26.3% and 34.8%, while the Malabar Botanical Garden recorded 27% and 40.1%, respectively. What the findings mean for conservation The study also examined 6,126 rescued orchids belonging to 12 regionally endemic species. Of these, 3,368 survived, translating to a survival rate of 55%. The group included eight species endemic to India and four shared between southern India and Sri Lanka. This was lower than the overall survival rate of 71.4%, highlighting the additional challenges involved in relocating species with more restricted natural distributions. The researchers found that some high-altitude and mist-forest-associated orchids also managed to survive and reproduce after being moved to lower elevations, although their establishment depended more on the receiving site. Orchids of India Calanthe biloba Lindl. #Orchids #India #Conservation #Biodiversity @ForestDeptt @Sdg13Un https://t.co/mZDyHDj2Mc — Dr. Sanjeet Kumar (Ecologist) (@BiotechSanjeet) October 19, 2026 Beyond survival, the researchers also looked at whether the rescued orchids could reproduce in their new surroundings. They found capsules containing embryos among the relocated plants , indicating that some had progressed beyond simply adapting to their new locations. However, the team stresses that relocation is not a substitute for protecting natural habitats. It is an additional conservation measure for situations where the removal of orchid-bearing trees cannot be avoided. Before a tree is marked for felling to make way for a wider road, there may be dozens of plants growing quietly on its trunk and branches. For orchids, the loss of that tree can mean the loss of an entire habitat. Identifying these plants before construction begins can make room for infrastructure without overlooking the smaller ecosystems that depend on the trees being removed. Sources: 'When Roads Remove Trees, Conservation Must Move Fast: A Rescue Translocation Model for Keralam's Native Epiphytic Orchids' : By Mithun Venugopal , Pradeep N. Sukumaran, Viswambharan Sarasan, Published on 15 October 2026 'Distribution and Abundance of Native Orchids on Roadside Trees in a Global Biodiversity Hotspot' : By Viswambharan Sarasan, Mithun Venugopal, Ratheesh M. K. Narayanan,Sidharth S. Nair, andPradeep N. Sukumaran, Published on 19 August 2025

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Baby Elephant Rescue Zuri Thrives Months After Septic Tank Ordeal Reading Time: 3 minutes Baby elephant rescue Zuri has thrived for months at the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust’s Nairobi Nursery after nearly drowning in a septic tank in Kenya. Baby elephant rescue stories rarely end as well as Zuri’s. Found trapped inside a septic tank near Voi Safari Lodge in Kenya when she was just days old, the calf has spent the past months recovering at the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust’s nursery in Nairobi. Keepers now describe a confident, food-driven toddler who has already claimed the role of herd princess. Rescuers worked late into the night to free Zuri from the tank, a traumatic ordeal for any elephant calf, let alone one only days old. After a night of stabilization at the Trust’s nearby Voi facility, she was flown to the Nairobi Nursery for round-the-clock care. The Nairobi Nursery is the first stop in a rehabilitation journey that can stretch for more than a decade. Orphaned elephants typically arrive after losing their mothers to poaching, drought, conflict, or accidents like Zuri’s. Keepers assign each calf a dedicated human caregiver who stays close around the clock, standing in for the mother an orphan has lost. Each baby elephant rescue brings its own logistical demands. Calves depend on a specialized milk formula that took decades of trial and error to perfect, since cow’s milk alone proved fatal to earlier generations of rescued elephants. Round-the-clock bottle feeding, veterinary monitoring, and a rotating team of keepers all continue for months or years after a calf first arrives. Within days of arriving, Zuri settled into the nursery herd and quickly displaced an older calf as the group’s most doted-on member. Several older orphans now compete to shepherd her around, with one in particular walking her into her stable each evening for weeks, until Zuri felt ready to go in alone. Keepers describe Zuri as anything but timid. She reportedly bangs on her stable door the moment she hears a wheelbarrow of milk bottles approaching at night, and sprints toward keepers with her trunk raised during the day, visibly displeased if a bottle isn’t ready and waiting. She has even tried stealing bottles from an older herd mate after finishing her own. Despite her boldness, Zuri shows a softer side around the nursery’s newest arrival, a recently rescued calf not yet publicly introduced. Keepers say Zuri doesn’t treat the newcomer as a rival the way she does with some of the older toddlers, a distinction they see as a promising sign of her continued emotional development. Bold enough to bang on her stable door at feeding time and steal milk bottles from herd mates, Zuri also shows a gentler side with the nursery’s newest arrival, a sign keepers read as promising emotional growth in the baby elephant rescue. Photo courtesy of Sheldrick Wildlife Trust . Not every trace of the ordeal has faded. Zuri remains wary of unfamiliar people and some of her own keepers, a caution the Trust attributes to her brush with drowning and the fear she experienced during the traumatic rescue. Recovery from early trauma varies widely between individual elephants, and keepers say patience, gentle care, reassurance, and close observation, rather than a fixed timeline, guide each calf’s progress. Over time, they hope Zuri will continue building confidence and feel increasingly secure in her new environment. Zuri’s progress reflects decades of institutional experience behind this kind of baby elephant rescue work. The Sheldrick Wildlife Trust has run its elephant rescue and rehabilitation program since the 1970s, hand-raising hundreds of orphans and successfully returning most to wild herds in Tsavo. Public support directly funds this kind of work. Individual donors can foster a specific orphan, supporting a program that covers keeper salaries, milk formula, and veterinary costs for calves like Zuri. That funding model has let the Trust scale its operations even as new rescue calls keep coming in from across Kenya. Around three years old, Zuri will eventually graduate from the nursery to one of the Trust’s reintegration units in Tsavo, following the same path generations of orphans before her took. For now, her days are filled with milk, mischief, and the attention of a devoted entourage of nannies. For a calf whose baby elephant rescue began three months ago with a near-drowning in a septic tank, that counts as a very good life. The post Baby Elephant Rescue Zuri Thrives Months After Septic Tank Ordeal appeared first on Happy Eco News .
