items.descriptionOriginal: A s a taxi driver, Juan Barbosa should in theory be one of the strongest opponents of a crackdown on cars. But, puffing on a cigarette beside his vehicle on a sultry August afternoon, the inhabitant of Pontevedra, Spain, admits that he finds himself in something of an existential crisis. “As a driver, I suffer,” says Barbosa, who has been ferrying passengers around the northwestern city for two decades. “We can’t enter certain areas unless we have a customer or a booking. We have to take longer routes. But as a pedestrian, life is better. I enjoy it when there are fewer vehicles around.” Post-pandemic, pedestrian-first urban planning is now all the rage, from 15-minute cities to low-traffic zones and the rise of soft mobility ( human-powered or low-emission electric transport). But Pontevedra, which is home to 85,000 people in the city and just under a million in the province, was way ahead of the curve. It technically began its war on cars last century. (In 1999, to be precise.) The urban transformation of Pontevedra was carried out gradually, over the course of several years. Credit: Peter Yeung Today Pontevedra, which fittingly is located on one of the world-famous Camino de Santiago pilgrimage routes , is considered perhaps the greatest example in the world when it comes to getting rid of cars. Every year, delegations of mayors, professors and city planners make their own pilgrimage to learn about this great vanishing act. “Pontevedra is an influential example and something we speak of often,” says Mark Nieuwenhuijsen , director of the urban planning, environment and health initiative at ISGlobal, a public health research institute based in Barcelona. “Many cities are now following their direction: It reduces air pollution, noise, and livability improves.” Over the course of the 20th century, the city came to be dominated by vehicles. By the late 1990s, an average of 80,000 cars drove through Pontevedra every day — astonishingly, according to the municipality, three times more than through Madrid and five times more than London. Many of these vehicles weren’t even heading for the city, but rather transiting to other destinations such as beach towns on the coast. Those that did stay would turn the city’s charming historic squares into parking lots. Pontevedra before it was redesigned for pedestrians. Credit: Council of Pontevedra This came at a cost. Pontevedra’s epoch of cars dirtied the air, led to the deaths of pedestrians and seized centuries-old public spaces from residents. “The city was loud, disagreeable, unlivable,” says Miguel Anxo Fernández Lores, the longstanding mayor of Pontevedra, from the desk of his city hall office. “All the roads were filled with cars. The city was like a huge, permanent traffic jam.” Fernández Lores, a doctor by trade, decided enough was enough. In 1999, he campaigned to reclaim Pontevedra’s streets. The population agreed and elected him. Yet the urban transformation was not overnight. It has been carried out gradually. Fernández Lores began with a major effort to keep unnecessary cars out of the historic city center, removing significant amounts of on-street parking and only allowing essential vehicles to enter. Within one month in office, he had pedestrianized 300,000 square meters of the city center. In other parts of the city, he narrowed roads and widened sidewalks, introduced 30 kilometer per hour speed limits citywide, down from 50 kilometers per hour, and began installing traffic-calming measures like raised pedestrian crosswalks as well as almost 300 speed bumps. To take one example, the central Benito Corbel Street once had four lanes of traffic. In 2000, that was reduced to two lanes with widened sidewalks and trees. By 2014, it became a single-track road with only service vehicles able to enter, and even then for a limited time. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] The mayor, who passed a Traffic and Mobility Plan for Pontevedra in 2011 formalizing and defining his pedestrian-first approach, also developed infrastructure to make it easier to ditch cars. The city now has roughly 4,500 private underground parking spaces and about 3,500 free “park and ride” spaces, all within a short walking distance from the center. Traffic lights were replaced by roundabouts to facilitate the flow of the remaining vehicles. In some central areas, the speed limit was lowered to just 10 kilometers per hour. Trees, green spaces and street lighting were also added to improve livability. But despite its reputation, Pontevedra is not completely car-free — it allows certain vehicles on its streets within reason. “It’s not a city without cars,” says Fernández Lores. “But we only let the ones that really need to come here in.” Miguel Anxo Fernández Lores, the longstanding mayor of Pontevedra. Credit: Peter Yeung Residents can drive to garaged parking spots in the city. People with disabilities are free to drive in Pontevedra as long as they have a permit. And vehicles used for emergencies and public services such as garbage and water trucks and ambulances are permitted 24/7. Home deliveries, house moving and loading and unloading by businesses are allowed, but only during certain hours. And indeed, taxi drivers like Barbosa may enter certain zones if they have a client or booking. When necessary, police can issue fines of several hundred euros, ensuring these limits are respected. “I think it was very smart, the decisions they made,” says Mirian Calvo , a researcher and expert in urban design from Pontevedra. “And this philosophy, of mixed-traffic, prioritizing soft mobility, has been applied over 30 years, more or less.” The results of Pontevedra’s policy to prioritize pedestrians in public spaces, sustained over more than a quarter of a century, are nothing short of stunning. Car trips in the city center have fallen by 97 percent, according to official municipal figures. The air is markedly cleaner, with CO2 emissions dropping by about 70 percent. And the streets are much safer: There have been no traffic deaths since 2011, whereas between 1996 and 2006, 30 people died in traffic accidents. (Pontevedra has won European road safety awards in the process.) The streets of Pontevedra have gotten much safer: There have been no traffic deaths since 2011. Credit: Pilar Picas / Shutterstock In fact, about 90 percent of all journeys in the city center are by foot, with road safety so high that 80 percent of kids aged 6 to 12 walk without their parents to school each morning. Many local business owners have signed up to be supervisors if the children need help for any reason. For all the talk of the climate and safety benefits that come with limiting vehicle traffic and designing pedestrian-first urban spaces, however, there has been a surprising further advantage: Pontevedra is thriving economically. While in the 1990s, retail activity was drifting towards the suburbs, the decision to prioritize a compact, walkable city with a high quality of life, has changed the picture drastically. The mayor, for his part, has rejected proposals to build malls on the urban periphery, protecting the pedestrian-oriented urban core. “We don’t want huge malls, we want small, independent businesses,” says Fernández Lores. Pontevedra is now the fastest-growing city in the region of Galicia and in recent years has attracted 15,000 new inhabitants, mostly young families from elsewhere in northwest Spain. It also generates more jobs per capita than any other city in the region. The results of Pontevedra’s policy to prioritize pedestrians in public spaces, sustained over more than a quarter of a century, are nothing short of stunning. Credit: Peter Yeung “It’s a very convenient city now,” says Calvo. “It’s a very nice city to live in and people can see that.” Most locals are effusive in their praise. Esther Louzao, 68, says that her home near Plaza Pelegrina was once surrounded by cars, but not anymore. She has even stopped driving to work, instead opting to go by bus. But she keeps her car for beach days. “I like it a lot, it’s easier to walk,” says Louzao, fittingly waiting at a bus stop. Pacing down the street with a stroller, Anna, a 39-year-old with a toddler son who lives four kilometers out of town, agrees. “It’s better, much safer, it’s pleasant,” she explains. “Even if sometimes my journeys take a bit longer.” Yet not all residents are entirely convinced by the policy. Manuel, who has been living in Pontevedra for 40 years, believes the transformation has been overstated. He owns three cars: one for the city, one for going to the beach and a third for sport driving. “Yes, the city is a lot different to how it was before,” says Manuel. “But it’s not as perfect as it seems. Some of us still need cars.” In Spain, all municipalities with over 50,000 inhabitants are now required have a low emission zone, like this one in Santander. Credit: Scharfsinn / Shutterstock Calvo agrees, noting that Pontevedra’s public transit network is lacking, which means that elderly people suffer and that cars must be taken to the coastal beaches. A system like Rome’s fleet of electric minibuses in the historic center could be implemented, she says. And although the results of Pontevedra’s policy are hard to deny, Calvo, who is also a lecturer in participatory architecture, argues that the system could have been even more effective and popular if residents had been more involved in the process. In the 2000s, she says, there was significant opposition to the project, even if that has now disappeared due to the clearly positive impact. “I don’t think there has been serious public engagement,” she says. “There are more things that could be done to make it more participatory.” Nieuwenhuijsen, however, commends Pontevedra’s less confrontational approach, which presented the restriction of cars as about livability. “I think everyone would prefer places with less noise and less pollution,” he says. “It shouldn’t be about the war on cars, presented as punishing someone.” In 2019, Oslo became the first European capital to effectively make its city center car-free. Credit: OlgaVysh / Shutterstock In any case, cities across the world are following in Pontevedra’s pioneering footsteps. In 2019, Oslo became the first European capital to effectively make its city center car-free by removing on-street parking spaces and restricting access. Freiburg, Germany, has similarly transformed the district of Vauban into a car-free zone, banning on-street parking and introducing vehicle speed limits at walking pace on residential streets. And in 2022, the Spanish government approved a royal decree requiring all municipalities with over 50,000 inhabitants to have a low emission zone, and recommending the use of traffic-restricted areas like that of Pontevedra. Yet not every place can easily replicate Pontevedra’s success. Professor Nieuwenhuijsen admits the transformation of North American cities could be more challenging given their size and lack of density. “U.S. cities were built around the car,” he says. “You get a lot of sprawl. European cities are different, many were designed for walking and horse carriages.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Likewise, transforming larger cities will not be as easy. Redesigning urban areas could be slowed or halted by infrastructure such as underground piping, adds Nieuwenhuijsen, and the investment required could prove prohibitive. Barcelona’s Superblocks cost as little as €500,000 but as much as €10 million per unit in some cases. But Fernández Lores, who is planning to run for an eighth term in 2027, believes that bigger cities could begin shifting away from cars and towards pedestrians by focusing on districts rather than entire cities. A case in point: In 2023, Culdesac Tempe, Arizona, became the first purpose-built, entirely car-free residential neighborhood in the U.S. “Cities work without cars,” he says. “But each city must find its own way.” The post The City That Kicked Out Cars Before It Was Cool appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Meet the Southeastern Gentoo, a New Penguin Species Discovered on the Kerguelen Islands Reading Time: 3 minutes Genomes from 64 gentoo penguins show the familiar bird is really four species, including the southeastern gentoo, a new penguin species discovered on the Kerguelen Islands. New penguin species discovered on the Kerguelen Islands? It is rare news in the penguin world. Yet the southeastern gentoo penguin is the first living penguin species named in more than a century. The Kerguelen Islands are a remote, windswept French territory in the southern Indian Ocean. Gentoo penguins have nested there for thousands of years. Until now, no one realized the local birds were their own species. Gentoos are easy to spot. They have a white patch above each eye and a bright orange bill. They are also among the fastest-swimming penguins. For more than a century, scientists treated all gentoos as one widespread species. Some proposed as many as six subspecies, but experts never agreed. A new genetic study now settles the debate. Communications Biology published the study in September 2026. Daly Noll, a graduate student at the University of Chile, led the genetic analysis. Senior authors came from Andrés Bello National University in Chile and the University of California, Berkeley. The team sequenced the full genomes of 64 penguins from 10 breeding colonies. Those colonies span almost the entire gentoo range. The researchers also compared body size, calls, diets, and breeding schedules. Scientists from about a dozen countries helped identify the new penguin species discovered on the Kerguelen Islands. Contributors came from Australia, South Africa, France, Brazil, and beyond. The data revealed four distinct species. The northern gentoo lives on the Falkland Islands and near South America. The eastern gentoo breeds on Crozet, Marion, and Macquarie islands. The southern gentoo occupies the Antarctic Peninsula, coastal Antarctica, and South Georgia. The fourth is the southeastern gentoo ( Pygoscelis kerguelensis ). It lives on the Kerguelen Islands and probably on nearby Heard Island too. Biologists call the southeastern gentoo a cryptic species. It looks almost identical to its relatives, and its differences lie mainly in its genes. Its body size and calls also differ subtly. This new penguin species discovered on the Kerguelen Islands has a relatively small population. That makes accurate classification especially important for its protection. The four species began to split between 300,000 and 500,000 years ago. Island isolation played a major role. The Antarctic Polar Front, an ocean boundary where water temperature and salinity change sharply, also played a role. Island isolation and the Antarctic Polar Front helped drive the evolution of four distinct species over hundreds of thousands of years. Photo by Antoine Lamielle on Wikimedia Commons. Gentoos also tend to return to the same colonies year after year. Over time, this loyalty to home kept populations apart. Each group then adapted to its own conditions. A flexible diet helped too. Gentoos eat fish, krill, squid, and cuttlefish, so each population could thrive on whatever its local waters offered. The genomes show those adaptations clearly. Southern gentoos carry genes for heat production and fat storage, while eastern gentoos carry genes for diving. Northern gentoos carry genes linked to digestion and heart function. Dr. Jane Younger of the University of Tasmania first proposed the split in a 2020 paper. Her team later examined museum specimens and found consistent physical differences between regions. She says the new study provides in-depth evidence to support that claim. Why does this matter beyond the name? Treating gentoos as one species produced an overall positive trend. That average hid serious declines in some regions. Southern gentoos on the Antarctic Peninsula are thriving and spreading south. In the Falklands, avian influenza has hit northern gentoos hard in recent years. Populations on Macquarie Island are declining. Climate change raises the stakes for each species. Under a moderate warming scenario, sub-Antarctic gentoos could lose suitable habitat on all their current islands by 2050. Few nearby islands offer alternatives. Antarctic gentoos may fare better and could even expand their range. Emperor, Adélie, and chinstrap penguins, however, are expected to decline as sea ice shrinks and krill supplies change. Other threats include warming seas, introduced rats and dogs, competition with fisheries, and capture in fishing gear. Recognizing each species allows conservation plans to match the threats each one faces. Researchers are already taking next steps. Senior author Juliana Vianna is studying penguin genomes for traits linked to surviving avian influenza. The team has also asked taxonomic authorities to review the split formally. Conservation bodies will need to assess each species separately. That work will determine how much protection the new penguin species discovered on the Kerguelen Islands receives. A bird seen in countless photos and documentaries turned out to hold hidden diversity . Careful genetic work revealed it. The new penguin species discovered on the Kerguelen Islands shows how much remains to be learned about familiar wildlife. The post Meet the Southeastern Gentoo, a New Penguin Species Discovered on the Kerguelen Islands appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s a particular feeling that comes with lifting the lid off the holiday storage bin. The tangle of lights, the ornament with the chipped corner, the little ceramic village you’ve set up on the same shelf for as long as you can remember. It’s comforting, and there’s a reason traditions stick around. But somewhere around the third box, the comfort can start to tip into a sort of déjà vu, and you might catch yourself wondering whether it’s time to start over. Before you head to the store, though, try a different idea. The holiday decorations you already own can look surprisingly different with a little rearranging, a few things from outside, and a willingness to break your own habits. Here are six ways to do it, whether you’re decking the halls for Thanksgiving , Christmas, Hanukkah or all of the above. Rethinking where holiday decorations go Give every piece a new home Most of us decorate on autopilot. The wreath goes on the same hook, the nativity scene lands on the same bookshelf, and the whole house ends up looking exactly like it did last year, because it is exactly like last year. This time, pause before you put anything down. Hold each piece and ask where else it could live. That nativity scene might feel brand new on the entryway table, where it’s the first thing people see. If you’re stuck, give yourself a rule: everything that usually goes upstairs goes downstairs this year, and vice versa. Choose one theme and edit to fit it Instead of pulling out every decoration you own, pick a theme and use only what matches. It can be as simple as one color, like all greens, or one motif, like snowflakes or anything that sparkles. Leaving some favorites in the box for a year can make them feel special again when they come back out, and the pieces you do use will look more intentional together. Bringing in natural and handmade touches Decorate with what’s growing outside Your backyard or a neighborhood walk can fill in a lot of gaps at no cost. A handful of pinecones lined along the mantel, or a few bare branches standing tall in a big vase on the kitchen island, adds texture and makes the familiar pieces around them look fresher. Dried citrus is another easy one. Slice oranges or grapefruit thin, dry them in a low oven until they turn translucent, and string them into a garland. Any extra slices make a lovely garnish for a winter drink. Add something your family made Handmade decorations carry a warmth store-bought ones can’t match. You could decide that this is the year the tree only gets ornaments made at the kitchen table, or have everyone in the house paint their own candle for the menorah. The pieces don’t need to be perfect. The slightly lopsided ones tend to become the favorites. Small changes to familiar holiday decor Trade your lights around String lights are easy to move, so let them wander. Bring the indoor lights outside and the outdoor ones in, or take the strand that usually wraps the tree and frame a doorway with it instead. Before anything goes outside, check that it’s rated for outdoor use, since indoor lights left out in the weather can become a fire hazard. Paint, mix and remake If you’re truly tired of a piece, change how it looks. Spray paint a set of old ornaments in a new color, hand-paint plain candles, or combine figures from two or three mismatched nativity sets into one scene. Experimenting is low-risk here. If you end up disliking the result, you were already ready to retire it, and if you love it, you’ve got something that feels new without buying a single thing, which might be the nicest kind of holiday surprise there is. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Bored of your holiday decorations? 6 ways to make old holiday decorations feel new first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Women in England and Wales who were arrested, cautioned or convicted for ending their own pregnancies no longer carry those records. Automatic abortion pardons took effect on November 16, and police and courts must now delete the details of past convictions, cautions, arrests and investigations wherever they can. The women affected don’t need to apply, pay a fee, or contact anyone. The pardons come under Section 242 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026 , passed earlier this year alongside a separate provision that removed women from criminal law for ending their own pregnancies. Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi, who brought forward the decriminalization amendment, says the change will clear the names of more than 100 women who were “unnecessarily harmed” by an “outdated” law. How the abortion pardons work Records deleted, or treated as deleted The pardon applies to abortion offenses relating to a woman’s own pregnancy, including cases where she acted beyond the legal time limits. Where full deletion from police and court systems isn’t possible, records must be marked so they are treated as erased. Alex Davies-Jones, the minister for victims and tackling violence against women and girls , said the pardons had been a priority. “Women do not have to take any direct action themselves, but can find out more information online and contact our dedicated casework team,” she said. What remains illegal The change ends prosecution of women over their own pregnancies, but abortion itself is still regulated. In England and Wales, abortion with an authorized provider is legal up to 24 weeks, with narrow exceptions after that point, such as when the mother’s life is at risk or the baby would be born with a severe disability. Medication taken at home is permitted before 10 weeks. Doctors and anyone else who act outside the Abortion Act 1967 can still face charges. Ending a Victorian law’s reach Nicola Packer’s five-year ordeal The law that the change dismantles dates to 1861, and the cases brought under it in recent years show what it meant in practice. In 2020, during a Covid lockdown, Nicola Packer, then 41, was prescribed abortion medication by phone through the National Health Service. She believed she was a few weeks pregnant. In fact, she was around 26 weeks along. Her friend Helle Tumbridge, speaking to the BBC with Packer’s consent, said she had experienced what’s known as a cryptic pregnancy. “That’s when you don’t have any sign of a pregnancy, no baby bump, no other symptoms,” she said. After a stillbirth, Packer went to the hospital, and staff called the police. “She was arrested. She spent a time in her hospital room recovering with two police officers present, one was a man. She was treated appallingly,” Tumbridge said. It took five years of investigation before a jury unanimously cleared her. “Of course, by that point the damage had been done, and she’ll live with that trauma for the rest of her life,” Tumbridge said. The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists said at the time that her trial showed “just how outdated and harmful” the law was. Reactions to the pardons Providers and advocates Heidi Stewart of the abortion care provider BPAS acknowledged that a pardon has limits. “While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice,” she said. Opponents of decriminalization Not everyone sees the change that way. Anti-abortion groups opposed both decriminalization and the pardons, arguing that removing criminal penalties, including for abortions late in pregnancy, leaves the unborn without legal protection. John Deighan, CEO of the Society for the Protection of Unborn Children, said in April that the pardons law “disgraces the children who have been needlessly destroyed in the past.” For the women whose records are now being cleared, the practical effect will show up in background checks, job applications, and travel paperwork that no longer carry a conviction or arrest. Antoniazzi and other supporters will be watching how smoothly police and courts carry out the deletions in the months ahead, since the pardon only works if the paperwork follows. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: An evocative shot of a waterfall of fog spilling into the sea in Mallorca, Spain, took the top honor in the Royal Meteorological Society’s 2026 Weather Photographer of the Year competition. Francisco Bailón Rodríguez captured the image during dawn’s first light, the rising sun illuminating the mist. “There’s a fabulous sense of flow in this image,” competition judge Angela Nicholson said in a statement. “The clouds are transformed into a river flowing over the cliffs. Francisco’s choice of exposure has captured the movement of the clouds perfectly below a beautiful sky with subtle color transitions.” Now in its second decade, the competition highlights the beauty and power of weather while raising awareness of the environmental issues that threaten life on Earth — things like heat, fires, and floods. Thirty images were shortlisted from a pool of over 5,500 taken in 13 countries. In addition to Rodríguez’s shot, eight photos were recognized as winners or runners-up across four categories: public vote, mobile, climate, and main. “These breathtaking images showcase the weather and climate in its pure beauty, complexity, and intensity,” said Liz Bentley, chief executive of the Royal Meteorological Society, per SWNS, adding: “Crucially, many of these images also deliver a powerful and urgent message about the global impact of climate change on environments ranging from parched agricultural land to melting ice caps.” The annual competition is free to enter and open to photographers of all ages and abilities, with judges looking for images that combine skill, meteorological observation, and storytelling. Take a look at the other winners and runners-up, with captions courtesy of contest organizers. Public Vote | Winner “Misty Sunrise Over the Long Coc Tea Hills” by Mahmudul Hasan Mahmudul Hasan/RMetS/SWNS “Captured in the delicate light of dawn, this breathtaking photo reveals the rolling tea hills of Long Coc, Vietnam, emerging through layers of mist.” Mobile Category | Winner “A Winter Morning” by Aung Soe Min Aung Soe MinRMetS/SWNS “A calm winter morning reveals Kuthodaw Pagoda rising through the mist and fog. Aung Soe Min captured the sun rays filtering across the landscape, creating a beautiful sunrise that captures the warmth of the weather and the peaceful serenity of this sacred site in Myanmar.” Climate Award | Winner “Fire” by Erfan Samanfar Erfan Samanfar/RMetS/SWNS “From Marvdasht, Iran, in October 2025, Erfan Samanfar captured a striking image of a farmer attempting to protect their land as fire spreads across the landscape.” Main Category | Runner-Up “Sunrise and Morning Glow” by Weilu Chen Weilu ChenRMetS/SWNS “As the sun rose over the Hong Kong Zhuhai-Macao Bridge, the morning sky was transformed into a spectacular display of golden light.” Public Vote | Runner-Up “Triple Strike NYC” by Dan Martland Dan Martland/RMetS/SWNS “Talk about being in the right place at the right time. From Bayonne, New Jersey, Dan Martland captured this spectacular scene overlooking the New York City skyline, as three lightning strikes lit the sky above the city.” Mobile Category | Runner-Up “A Rainbow Over Loch Duck” by Anthony Bird Anthony BirdRMetS/SWNS “Framed by the rolling hills and water below, a magnificent rainbow arches across the landscape of Loch Duck, Scotland. The scene caught Anthony Bird’s eye so quickly that there was barely time to think, as he simply had to ‘run outside the Airbnb’ to capture it.” Climate Award | Runner-Up “Castles in the Wind” by Andres Miraglia Andres Miraglia/RMetS/SWNS “As an iceberg drifted away from the glacier that released it in Antarctica’s Paradise Harbour, Andres Miraglia captured the moment against a pristine sunset.” Main Category | Third Place “A Supercell in the Sandhills of Nebraska” by Laura Hedien Laura Hedien/RMetS/SWNS “While out storm chasing in the Nebraska sandhills, ‘Mother Nature was kind enough to give us a supercell and lightning at night,’ explains Laura Hedien.” This article was originally written by Dean Murray for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets .

items.descriptionOriginal: A family in Los Angeles’ Lake Balboa neighborhood has a holiday tradition that dates back about 80 years. Every Thanksgiving, the host and a helper write “Turkey Notes” for all the loved ones attending the feast. The only rule? Include the word “turkey” somewhere in the text. The notes range from silly rhymes (“Turkey red, turkey yellow, turkey says you’re an awesome fellow”) to sincere celebrations of guests’ recent accomplishments. The writers then wrap the notes in colorful tissue paper and “roll them like a Tootsie Roll with ribbon on each end,” Nice News reader Sadie shared, adding that the ritual makes for some of her favorite memories. Sadie is one of the dozens of readers who answered our call earlier this month to submit the seasonal family traditions they partake in. Multiple made us laugh out loud, while others were deeply touching. We rounded up a selection for you to peruse — and they just might inspire new shared activities for your own holiday gatherings. Iuliia Anisimova—iStock/Getty Images Plus The hood ornament from my husband’s mother’s car he wrecked as a teenager. It was his only Christmas gift that year. It’s the first ornament we hang every year. – Katherine (Lake Wylie, South Carolina) Thanksgiving Eve, we have a family/friend gathering called BAGG, which stands for Bucket-A-Go-Go. We started this tradition because my husband was tired of eating turkey on Thanksgiving and wanted a change. Nobody wanted to change the Thanksgiving menu, so BAGG was created! Every family brings their own meal but the No. 1 rule is that it must NOT be turkey! The tradition started with a bucket of chicken but now it is whatever the family brings (but NO turkey). One year someone brought a turkey sandwich and they were booed! – Lauren (Roanoke, Virginia) Cookies! We have a cookie trade! Everyone bakes two to three different types of cookies and then we get together for a Christmas party and eat cookies while spending time together. At the end of the get-together, we all split up the cookies so everyone gets to take home a few of each type of cookie. – Stacy (La Mesa, California) My three children were young when their dad and I divorced. He lived in a different state and this meant the children were always torn between celebrating Thanksgiving and Christmas with either mom or dad. So the children and I invited our exclusive holiday — Thanksmas — which was celebrated in early December. We decorated with both fall and Christmas decorations, cooked a meal of Thanksgiving and Christmas dishes, and enjoyed holiday music. And they never had to decide between celebrating Thanksmas with mom or dad each year — it was ours, and ours alone! – Norine (Winchester, Virginia) In our family, we write funny clues on the gifts. While opening them, we read the clues aloud and try to guess what the gift is. – Jennifer (Duluth, Minnesota) My brother sent me an orange tree the year our dad died. Purple and orange were his favorite colors, so I decorated it with purple ornaments. It now goes up in October and transitions from a Halloween tree with bats to a Thanksgiving tree with turkey hands made by my 10 grandchildren, and then to the Christmas tree. Reminders of both my dad and my thoughtful brother. – Debra (Olathe, Kansas) I love putting out my holiday decorations from my favorite holidays, Diwali and Thanksgiving to Christmas. I also celebrate my decorations every year inside my house trying new styles as I desire after talking with my household for what we all like most. – Sautam (Massachusetts) Every year my husband and I host “Nacho Christmas.” It came about because we both wanted a chill holiday with plenty of quality time with any friends and family that want to stop through. We set up the nacho bar so people can eat whenever they come by — no need to coordinate a meal at a set time. … It’s such a huge hit that a friend had a terrible nightmare where I told her she can’t come anymore and she woke up crying. Nacho Christmas for the win. – Wendy (Chicago, Illinois) My son and I watch a holiday movie every night, beginning with Miracle on 34th Street on Thanksgiving Eve. We will have the tree up and lit as well, and then add a few ornaments every day. We always save a few so friends and family can hang something when they come over. Of course we go to see the tree at Rockefeller Center and the Rockettes every year as well! – Peggy (New York City) Making Aebleskivers, a Danish round ball pancake, on Christmas morning. They are the size of a golf ball and you make them in a pan with round holes. When the bottom of the pancake is cooked, you turn it over to cook the top side using a knitting needle. When done they can be eaten as is or with powdered sugar or honey, or you can split them open and add jam, whipped cream, or pudding in the middle. It has been a family tradition for 100 years. – Kathy (Texas) Butterscotch Schnapps milkshakes. Ice cream, milk, and Schnapps. That’s it. Sit around, talk, and drink. It’s fantastic. – Emery (Saskatchewan, Canada) My family (me, my husband Tim, and our two sons: TJ, 22, and Joey, 18) saves all the holiday cards we receive throughout the season and open them all at once after dessert on Christmas Eve. We started this tradition about 10 years ago and it’s been a favorite of everyone’s. This way, Tim and I can share who our nonlocal friends are, but over time, our sons know them and recognize them, even if they’ve never met them in person. And it’s a good way for someone not to miss some important updates. We just wish more friends and families still sent out cards. We love them. – Amy (Poulsbo, Washington) Every year for Hanukkah when my kids were still at home, we made latkes, played games, lit candles, and invited friends over. Some years, instead of giving individual gifts, we did one big family experience together. When the kids were in their teens, we decided that the first of the eight nights would be dedicated to charity, so instead of exchanging presents, we bought them for others in need or made a donation. – Elaine (Baltimore, Maryland) While raising our children in New Hampshire, we had many winter days where we lost electricity because of ice/snow storms. When the kids were very young, we lost electricity one Christmas Eve. But having a wood stove as the primary way to heat the house, at least we were warm. So, for lighting, we placed lit candles in every room and cooked some basic foods on top of the wood stove. It was magical for the children. This started a tradition on every Christmas Eve of turning off all the lights in the house, lighting only candles, and eating just hors d’oeuvres — which we have now done for 30-plus years. – Jim (North Carolina) Every Christmas, I plan a solo trip that I look forward to all year. I try to fly on Christmas Day and bring a little gift (usually a box of chocolates) for the flight attendants. While flying on the holiday tends to be a little less expensive, the real benefit is that people are kinder and more patient with one another. It reminds me of the airport scene at the beginning of Love Actually . – Marie (Frankfurt) My father is a Methodist minister. When he was in seminary shortly after World War II, he attended a Christmas party. A warm punch was served and he really liked it. He obtained the recipe and we’ve made the wassail punch every year since! We still have the original typed recipe on crinkly typewriter paper. – Carol (Alameda, California) Fruitcakes. Every Halloween weekend, I make fruitcakes with raisins, currants, apricots, pecans, cinnamon, clove, mace, and, yes, some of the traditional citron but less. Sherry and brandy poured over them every weekend until the weeks between Thanksgiving and Christmas. My paternal grandmother kept them in her pantry and I loved to watch her take them out, unwrap the wax paper, and pour sherry through cheesecloth then re-wrap and set on the self. She is with me all the time I make these. – Susan Conklin (Hood River, Oregon) My two sons are grown now, but when they were small they would make an ornament for the tree. The early ones were simple, a scrap of fabric (I had to sew the seams as they were only 2 and 4 years old), stuffed little pillows with fluffy cotton. As the years went by, the ornaments became quite amazing for little hands. As a 4-year-old, my youngest was able to complete a framed cross stitch on his own. This was a tradition until they each left for college. I now hang about 30 wildly creative ornaments on my own tree. – Ki’ihele (Hawai’i) Making gifts for my family and my friends, be it knitted mittens, a painting, or special desserts, while I enjoy the winter scenery outside my kitchen window. – Dianne (River Falls, Wisconsin) About a decade ago, I began a tradition with my son (now 13) that we call the thankful tree. I found a little decorative tree and we have leaf-shaped papers with string. Every night of November, we each write down something we are grateful for from that day, share them out loud, and hang them on the tree. By the end of the month, our tree (and hearts) are bursting with gratitude, and I save and label the “leaves” from each year, so we can look back on memories and gratitude. – Sarah (Denver, Colorado) I am one of 10 children. When we were born, my mother knit us a Christmas stocking with our names on it. As we married and had children, she knit stockings for our spouses and her grandchildren. My brother-in-law built a faux fireplace that we keep at the Elks Club. We get together every Christmas Eve and hang our stockings! There are usually 40-50 stockings! – Mary (Warren, New Jersey) Every December, we delight in attending a carol service at a huge old church on Bloor St. — a main street in the downtown. People put twenties on the collection plate which goes entirely to support the Toronto Star Santa Claus Fund begun by newspaper editor Joe Atkinson so underprivileged children would receive a Christmas gift. Boxes contain mitts, warm hats, books, candy, etc. This was especially welcomed during the Great Depression and continues the spirit of giving to this day! – Gail (Toronto, Canada) Since college, my sibling and I have played Santa for our parents. It’s our way of giving back. Yes, our parents still play Santa for us, and Santa gifts are, dare I say, now more anticipated than family gifts. – Eli (Seattle, Washington) Every year, we rent a big house or conference center for around 20 family members. We bring a Ping-Pong table if need be and we play card games, board games, puzzles, and, of course, Ping-Pong. Wednesday night is cheese streak night. On Thursday, we all work to make the Thanksgiving meal. Friday we hike and play, play, play. It never gets old. This year we are trying a new location, the Jersey Shore. – Joyce (Ottsville, Pennsylvania) My grandmother’s favorite color was purple; she passed about 20 years ago. Each year for Christmas, my mom and I wrap a special package in purple paper to give to each other from my grandmom, Mabelle. – Kimberleigh (Maryland) RELATED: We Asked Readers to Share the Best Compliments They’ve Received

items.description: Κάθε Τρίτη, η σεφ του Τορόντο, Μάντι Γκόλντμπεργκ, δένει σε μια ποδιά στην τοπική τράπεζα τροφίμων και μεταμορφώνει ό,τι τυχαία συστατικά βρίσκει --κρεμμύδια, καρότα, ένα ξεχασμένο σακουλάκι με ωμές κόκκινες φακές -- σε 100 ζεστά γεύματα για οικογένειες που τα χρειάζονται. Το έργο ξεκινά από μια ήσυχη στιγμή απολογισμού κατά τη διάρκεια των χρόνων της στη βιομηχανία της εξαιρετικής εστίασης, όταν…
items.descriptionOriginal: Every Tuesday, Toronto chef Maddy Goldberg ties on an apron at her local food bank and transforms whatever random ingredients she finds -- onions, carrots, a forgotten bag of raw red lentils -- into 100 hot meals for families who need them. The work traces back to a quiet moment of reckoning during her years in the fine dining industry, when she finally asked herself a question more people might benefit from sitting with: "What can I actually do?" For Goldberg, the answer wasn't grand -- it was a free Tuesday and a phone call to a food bank. "I wanted to do something where the goal wasn't to make money off of it," she says. "It was just to feed people, which is why I wanted to cook in the first place." Her story is a small reminder that the gap between caring about something and actually doing something about it is often narrower than it appears.

items.title: Γεια σου! Χαμπάρι! Μάθετε πώς να πείτε γεια σε 25 διαφορετικές γλώσσες
items.titleOriginal: Halló! Habari! Learn How to Say Hello in 25 Different Languages
items.description: Το 1973, οι Αμερικανοί αδελφοί Μάικλ και Μπράιαν ΜακΚόρμακ έστειλαν 1.360 επιστολές σε επτά γλώσσες σε κυβερνητικούς ηγέτες σε όλο τον κόσμο, ενθαρρύνοντάς τους να συμμετάσχουν στην εναρκτήρια Παγκόσμια Ημέρα Γειας. «Θέλαμε να κάνουμε κάτι για να γιορτάσουμε τη σημασία της προσωπικής επικοινωνίας για τη διατήρηση της ειρήνης», δήλωσε ο Michael, ανώτερος υπάλληλος στο Χάρβαρντ εκείνη την εποχή, προηγ.…
items.descriptionOriginal: In 1973, American brothers Michael and Brian McCormack mailed 1,360 letters in seven languages to government leaders across the globe, encouraging them to participate in the inaugural World Hello Day. “We wanted to do something to celebrate the importance of personal communication to preserving peace,” Michael, a senior at Harvard at the time, previously told the university paper, The Crimson . He and Brian had pooled their money to pay for the postage, with the goal of getting their recipients to agree to, quite literally, spread the word. The idea behind the holiday, observed every Nov. 21, is that differences should be addressed through peaceful conversation rather than conflict. To participate, all you have to do is say “hello” to 10 people. Fifteen countries pledged their support the first year; today, individuals in 180 have joined in — including 31 Nobel Peace Prize winners who sent the brothers letters championing World Hello Day. “It’s something people can do on their own in widely different places,” Michael explained to the Associated Press back in 1991. “It gives people a chance to do something about the world; it empowers them.” Ready to get started? Before you do, consider broadening your reach by learning how to say hello in a few different languages — below are 25 translations (plus two bonus ones, just for fun). Portuguese – olá Hindi – namaste Dutch – hallo Filipino – kumusta Ukrainian – pryvit Arabic – marhaban Polish – witam Greek – geiá sou Hebrew – shalom Mandarin – nǐ hǎo Spanish – hola Esperanto – saluton Yoruba – pẹlẹ o Hawaiian – aloha Japanese – kon’nichiwa Icelandic – halló Swahili – habari French – bonjour Zulu – sawubona Korean – annyeonghaseyo Persian – salām Turkish – merhaba Swedish – hej Samoan – talofa Italian – ciao Klingon (from Star Trek ) – nuqneH Dothraki (from Game of Thrones ) – m’athchomaroon

items.title: 5 τρόποι που το λογισμικό Healthcare SaaS υποστηρίζει περισσότερες βιώσιμες επιχειρηματικές πρακτικές
items.titleOriginal: 5 Ways Healthcare SaaS Software Supports More Sustainable Business Practices
items.description: Happy Eco News 5 τρόποι που το λογισμικό Healthcare SaaS υποστηρίζει περισσότερες βιώσιμες επιχειρηματικές πρακτικές Χρόνος ανάγνωσης: 8 λεπτά 5 τρόποι που το λογισμικό Healthcare SaaS υποστηρίζει περισσότερες βιώσιμες επιχειρηματικές πρακτικές Η υγειονομική περίθαλψη παρήγαγε περίπου το 8,5 τοις εκατό όλων των εκπομπών αερίων του θερμοκηπίου στις ΗΠΑ το 2018, σύμφωνα με μια ανάλυση του 2020 στον τομέα Health Affairs που θέτει…
items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News 5 Ways Healthcare SaaS Software Supports More Sustainable Business Practices Reading Time: 8 minutes 5 Ways Healthcare SaaS Software Supports More Sustainable Business Practices Health care produced roughly 8.5 percent of all US greenhouse gas emissions in 2018 , according to a 2020 analysis in Health Affairs that put the sector’s total at about 553 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent. My argument here is simple: healthcare SaaS, the software a clinic rents over the internet instead of running on its own machines, is one of the cheapest ways for a practice to shrink its share of that number, and most of the savings show up in the budget too. Now picture one family clinic. Behind the front desk sits a back room lined with manila folders, a shredding bin and a fax machine that still rattles every afternoon. Across the hall, a server closet hums all night with its door propped open because the room runs hot. That clinic is not a villain. It is just carrying what I call everyday carbon : the emissions that come from paper, idle servers, car trips and supplies that expire on a shelf. None of it is dramatic. All of it adds up, and almost all of it can be trimmed without touching a single clinical decision. I have spent years building and fixing software for clinics and hospitals, from appointment tools for two-doctor practices to records systems for regional hospital groups. The five changes below are the ones I have seen stick. 1. Paperless records and e-prescribing empty the archive room Before the switch, a typical small practice runs on paper that moves. Charts travel from the shelf to the exam room and back. Prescriptions get printed, signed, handed over, and sometimes lost in a coat pocket, which means a second trip for the patient. Old files go to an off-site storage unit, and someone drives there whenever a records request comes in. After the switch, the chart lives in a cloud-based electronic health record. A prescription goes straight from the doctor’s screen to the pharmacy, so there is no paper slip and no handwriting for the pharmacist to call about. Intake forms get filled out on a phone the night before instead of on a clipboard in the waiting room. What surprised me the first time I watched a practice go through this was where the real savings hid. The paper itself mattered less than the trips around it: courier runs to the storage unit, patients coming back for a forgotten form, staff driving boxes to a shredding service. One practice I worked with turned its old archive room into a third exam room within a year, which was the moment the owner stopped calling the project “the IT thing.” Nobody misses the fax machine. (Well, one office manager did, for about a week.) 2. A slice of a big data center beats a humming server closet The on-premise server is the quiet energy hog of small health care. It runs around the clock, needs its own cooling, gets replaced every few years, and in most clinics I have visited it sits mostly idle outside office hours. Backups often mean a second machine, or a drive someone takes home on Fridays. Large cloud data centers do the same work far more efficiently, and the numbers on this are striking. A Berkeley Lab analysis published in Science found that from 2010 to 2018, global data center computing output rose 550 percent while energy use rose only 6 percent , with most of the gains coming from big operators running highly efficient facilities. When a clinic moves its records, billing and scheduling to a SaaS product, it trades a single half-used box for a tiny, well-managed slice of one of those buildings. Off-the-shelf products cover most of what a typical clinic needs, but not everything. A fertility center with an unusual lab workflow, or a rural health network that wants its own patient app tied to existing systems, often ends up working with a partner that offers healthcare software development services to build the missing piece. My advice to anyone in that position is to make the green choices at the design stage: pick a cloud region on a cleaner power grid, decide how long logs and imaging files stay in fast storage before they move to cheaper cold storage, and stop the system from keeping five copies of the same scan. Building those rules in from day one costs very little. Retrofitting them into a live system full of patient data means migrations, compliance reviews and weekend downtime, and in my experience that costs far more. One pushback comes up in nearly every conversation I have about this. Skeptics raise a fair objection: the cloud does not cut emissions, it just moves them into giant data centers, and with AI pushing demand up, those buildings are only getting hungrier. Part of that is true. AI is driving a wave of new data center construction, and it deserves close scrutiny. But a clinic is not choosing between the cloud and zero emissions. It is choosing between the cloud and a lone server in a closet with a window air conditioner, and the Berkeley Lab work shows that the efficiency gains landed at the large operators. A clinic can also ask its vendor which region hosts its data and pick one on a cleaner grid, which is a settings change, not a construction project. 3. Telehealth takes car trips off the road without anyone noticing The most visible change is also the easiest to measure. Every follow-up visit that happens over video is a round trip that never happens, and for patients in rural areas that round trip can eat half a day. A national study published in The American Journal of Managed Care in 2025 looked at claims for 44.7 million insured US adults from April to June 2023. Scaled to the whole insured adult population, the researchers estimated that telemedicine averts between 21.4 million and 47.6 million kilograms of CO2 every month , roughly the monthly emissions of 61,000 to 130,000 gasoline cars. The authors call the effect modest relative to all of health care, and they are right to. Still, that is a cut that came almost entirely from visits people preferred anyway. In the practices I have worked with, the clinics that get the most from telehealth are the ones that decide on purpose which visits belong on video. Medication check-ins, test result reviews and most mental health sessions move online well. A sprained ankle does not. There is a second, smaller commute hiding in the same change. Once records, billing and scheduling live in the cloud, the people who handle them no longer have to sit next to the server. I have seen coding and billing teams move to two office days a week, which takes a few more cars off the road and frees up desk space the clinic was paying to heat and cool. The patient keeps the afternoon. The planet keeps the gas. 4. Smarter scheduling and inventory keep vials out of the trash Waste in a clinic is rarely one big mistake. It is a slow trickle of small ones: a box of supplies ordered twice because nobody checked the cabinet, a vaccine lot that expired behind a newer one, a refrigerator that failed on Saturday night and was found on Monday morning. Before SaaS, inventory usually lives in a spreadsheet or a clipboard that one person understands. Orders go out “just in case,” because running short feels worse than overbuying. After the switch, stock levels connect to the appointment calendar, so the system knows that next week has twelve flu shot appointments and only ten doses on hand. It flags lots that are close to expiring so staff use them first, and a cheap temperature sensor in the vaccine fridge sends an alert to a phone the minute something goes wrong. I once watched a pediatric practice lose a full fridge of vaccines to a weekend power fault. After they added a connected sensor, the next fault triggered a text at 2 a.m., a staff member drove in, and the doses moved to a backup unit before any of them warmed up. Nobody wrote a sustainability report about it. It was simply less waste. Scheduling tools help in a quieter way. Automated text reminders cut no-shows, which means fewer wasted slots and fewer rebooked trips. For home health teams, route planning groups nearby visits together, so nurses drive less and see more patients in a day. The software does not care about carbon at all. It cares about minutes and miles, and the carbon follows. 5. Remote monitoring keeps patients home and out of the ambulance The last change reaches past the clinic walls. Patients with heart failure, high blood pressure or diabetes can now send daily readings from a connected scale, blood pressure cuff or glucose meter, and a nurse sees a warning sign days before it becomes an emergency. Evidence from the research side is encouraging, though not unanimous. A 2025 meta-analysis in Cureus pooled 15 studies, nine of them randomized trials, and found that remote patient monitoring reduced heart failure hospitalizations , with the strongest effect from implanted monitors and a smaller one from simpler home devices. The authors rated their confidence in the hospitalization result as moderate, which is an honest grade for a field that is still maturing. Here is where I go a step further. Every avoided hospital stay also means an ambulance ride that did not happen, a bed that did not need heating and cooling for four days, and a stack of single-use supplies that never got opened. The meta-analysis did not count any of that, so this is my own extrapolation. But anyone who has seen how much material a single admission consumes will find it hard to argue the other way. For patients, the benefit is simpler. They sleep in their own beds. What changes when a clinic makes all five moves? Put side by side, the before and after look like this. Practice Before After with SaaS Records and prescriptions Paper charts, printed scripts, fax, off-site storage runs Cloud health record, e-prescriptions sent straight to the pharmacy IT infrastructure Server closet running around the clock with its own cooling Hosted in large data centers, where Berkeley Lab found compute grew 550 percent on 6 percent more energy (2010 to 2018) Routine visits Every follow-up means a car trip Suitable follow-ups on video, an estimated 21.4 to 47.6 million kg of CO2 averted each month across insured US adults (2023 data) Supplies and scheduling Overordering, expired stock, missed fridge failures, no-shows Stock tied to the calendar, expiry alerts, fridge sensors, automated reminders Chronic care Problems surface in the emergency room Daily readings from home, fewer heart failure hospitalizations in pooled studies None of these rows asks a clinic to become a climate organization. Each one is a normal operations upgrade that happens to shrink everyday carbon along the way. Where can a clinic start this quarter? You do not need a sustainability officer to begin. Most everyday carbon sits inside decisions a practice manager already makes, so the steps below fit into budgets and meetings that exist today. Count the paper before you cut it. Spend one week tracking what gets printed, faxed, couriered or driven anywhere. The list is usually shorter than people fear and points to two or three workflows worth moving online first. Start with whatever generates car trips, because those carry the biggest footprint. Ask every software vendor where your data lives. A good SaaS provider can tell you which cloud region hosts your records and whether that region runs on a cleaner grid. If your vendor cannot answer, that tells you something about how closely they watch their own infrastructure. The same question belongs in every new contract. Make video the default for follow-ups that do not need hands. Sit down with your clinicians and agree on a short list of visit types that start as virtual unless the patient prefers otherwise. Patients in rural areas will thank you first. Review the list every six months, since comfort with video tends to grow. Connect the supply room to the calendar. Even a basic inventory module that knows upcoming appointments will stop most double orders. Add a connected temperature sensor to any fridge that holds vaccines or biologics. It is one of the cheapest insurance policies a clinic can buy. Write a retention rule for data, not just for paper. Federal and state law set how long medical records must be kept, so start there, then decide what happens to everything else: old logs, duplicate image files, test exports. Data that nobody needs still sits on powered drives somewhere, and a clear rule keeps your cloud bill and your footprint from creeping upward. A greener clinic in 2030 might look like this What follows is a picture of what is possible, not a forecast. It is a Tuesday morning in 2030. The front desk has no printer. The room that once held folders is an exam room with a window, and the old server closet stores yoga mats for the staff wellness class. Half of today’s follow-ups happen on video, so the parking lot has empty spaces. A home nurse’s route was planned overnight, with four visits on the same side of town. In the vaccine fridge, every vial is in date, because the system flagged the oldest lot last week and the team used it first. Three heart failure patients sent their morning weights before breakfast, and one of them got a phone call and a medication adjustment instead of an ambulance ride. Nothing in that scene requires a breakthrough. Every piece of it exists today. The greenest clinic of 2030 will not look heroic, just quietly well organized. items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: A wristband developed at the University of Nottingham sends small electrical pulses to a nerve in your wrist, and for some people with Tourette’s, their tics settle within moments of switching it on. One 15-year-old called the first time she tried it the best day of her life. Arielle and Karissa also get into a Greek ship that turned seven years of beach trash into a pollution map, a cancer therapy helping people with Céline Dion’s rare condition walk again, and the real reason you want to cancel plans you were excited to make. Learn more about April Surac and NeuraSensa: https://www.instagram.com/neurasensa/ If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Anything more and you’re setting yourself up for feeling guilty for missing something on a certain morning, or if you have, like, a long checklist of things to do, then it can put a lot of pressure on you as well. Um, so yeah, I did also like that aspect of the article that really emphasizes that it doesn’t have to be complicated. We’re not going through all of the tips here, like what to do the night before, but I highly recommend you check out the article for some more morning routine inspo. Karissa: Yeah, 100%. “This Tourette’s wrist device cut tics by a quarter in a UK trial” Arielle: All right. The next solution is titled “This Tourette’s wrist device cut tics by a quarter in a UK trial.” There’s a wristband out of the University of Nottingham that sends tiny electrical pulses to a nerve in your wrist, and for some people with Tourette’s, it calms their tics the moment they switch it on. One 15-year-old called the first time she tried it the best day of her life. I actually have a cousin who has Tourette’s. And his tics are not so… They’re, they… Like, he can go through the world and navigate it fine, but you can tell that he’s putting a lot of energy towards suppressing a lot as well. Yeah. I can only imagine how life-changing a device like this is that’s kind of subtle and elegant and simple and has a really big impact on just the mental and physical space that suppressing tics has, and also just having to go through the world with people staring at you, not really understanding what’s going on. The source for this article came from the BBC, and I actually took a minute to watch their video on this, and I highly recommend watching the video so that you can kind of get a better sense for how much impact this small device has on people. Karissa: Yeah. And how exactly does it work? Arielle: So how it works is kind of wild. There’s rhythmic pulses to the median nerve cha- which changes activity in the parts of the brain that control movement. In a trial of 121 people, tics dropped by about 25% on average, and it even works for people who don’t have Tourette’s. There was another teenager named Ollie, and he has a functional neurological disorder which makes his neck move constantly without him having any control over it. And when he tried the device, it also just completely stopped the neck movements. There’s a lot of potential for this wearable neurotech to positively affect the lives of people with Parkinson’s tremors or anxiety or even OCD. “Animal welfare ballot measures had a strong night in the 2026 midterms” Arielle: The next solution is titled “Animal welfare ballot measures had a strong night in the 2026 midterms.” Okay, so we’ve already talked about the midterms, but we haven’t talked about this specific area of it. I think most people have never eaten foie gras in their lives, and yet it produced some of the most lopsided votes of election night. Animals came out of these midterms surprisingly well, and there’s a pattern in what passed and what didn’t that I found quite interesting. First of all, do you know how foie gras is made? Have you ever eaten it, Karissa? Karissa: Never eaten it, and I didn’t really know much about it until this article actually. Arielle: Yeah. I, I wanna say I have never tried it, but I can’t be for certain. I, I- worked a lot in the hospitality industry and, uh, tried a lot of different things, but it makes me feel a bit bad if I, if I had, because they basically, like, force feed ducks. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: Um, or is it geese? But they- I think it’s geese, yeah … force feed them, and it produces this pâté-like, um I’m not describing this well, but people who know foie gras, you know what I’m talking about. Yeah. And those of you who don’t, look it up ’cause it is a l- well, it’s kinda disturbing. Um, so DC voted 73% and Denver 66% to ban foie gras sales, and a DC chef has been hosting foie gras tasting dinners to fund a lawsuit against the ban. So, yeah. Oh. There’s a, a little bit of tension there. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: Colorado rejected a constitutional right to hunt and fish, and the fight came down to two words: traditional methods, which critics said could have brought back leg-hold traps and poison as, um, as hunting strategies. Denver voters said no to banning fur and slaughterhouses in 2024, but yes to banning foie gras now. So it seems like narrow bans on one practice seem to have a much easier time going through than ones that take on a whole industry for, of course, concerns about employment and yeah, having to restructure or get rid of a whole industry. Um- so more people are actually paying attention to how their food is produced, even when they’re not really changing their diet. Like, they’re not going vegan, they’re not going vegetarian, but they are concerned about how their food is produced and where it comes from. “The Greek coastline cleanup that turned trash into a pollution map” Arielle: The next solution is titled “The Greek coastline cleanup that turned trash into a pollution map.” The team that’s doing the cleanup isn’t just picking up trash. They’re noting down every single piece of it. This project consists of one ship, 20 people, five inflatable boats, and 1,140 tons of trash pulled off remote shores since 2019. For a visual, that’s 22 Olympic swimming pools’ worth of pollution. They’ve built what they say is the largest marine pollution database in the Mediterranean, and university researchers are using it to map plastic on the seabed. The data led them somewhere they didn’t necessarily expect. A lot of the trash came from inland, from rivers and illegal dumps, so they also started a second program on land. Beach cleanups are pretty popular, but there’s growing frustration that cleaning up the beach doesn’t necessarily stop the flow, or it doesn’t nip the issue in the bud. But it’s nice to see that citizen science and cleanup data are increasingly shaping policy on plastics. “April Surac built NeuraSensa so art adapts to the people using it” Arielle: The last solution that I’m going to share with you before I hand it over to Karissa is a Local Changemaker. This one’s titled “April Surac built NeuraSensa so art adapts to the people using it.” This week’s Local Changemaker is April Surac, a Florida teenager who grew up in her family’s furniture workshop and has a younger sister who has autism. Her installations are made of fabric with sensors built in, so the surfaces shift under your hand and the light and sound change as you move through the room. They’re designed for people with autism and people with sensory or cognitive differences, including dementia. More than 15,000 people have experienced the installations, and she sent over 250 sensory kits to families, schools, and hospitals. And she funds a lot of it with her own savings. I think she started this when she was only 16 or 17, which is so impressive. She’s also a 2025 Barron Prize winner, and she’s now working on gallery commissions in New York, LA, and London. Plus, she is developing a wearable sensory tool, and she’s moving towards patents for that. I think it’s really encouraging that a lot of people are growing in their awareness and compassion for diverse bodies and experiences. Sensory-friendly hours are popping up at museums, grocery stores, and movie theaters, which comes from people just realizing how much public spaces assume about our bodies. It’s wonderful to see the shift from accessibility compliance to designing for everyone from the very beginning of a project. Karissa: Yeah, exactly. And I really loved that she had a line that said, “Design should adapt to people, not the other way around.” And that’s something we don’t see enough of in our world. So I think this is just such a fascinating, uh, story, what she’s doing, and I feel so honored to be able to share her story here on The Optimist Daily as one of our local changemakers this year. “US homelessness decline hits its steepest one-year drop in a decade” Karissa: “US homelessness decline hits its steepest one-year drop in a decade.” So homelessness in the US dropped more than 6% last year. That’s about 49,000 fewer people without housing, and the biggest one-year drop in over a decade. One of the biggest points here in this article is that veteran homelessness is down nearly 60% since 2010, and advocates say it’s proof that putting people in housing first with no strings attached actually works. On the other hand, the Trump administration credits immigration enforcement and encampment crackdowns to this decline, but advocates say their data shows cities with camping bans did worse than average. It’s important to note, too, that not everyone saw a drop because people who’ve been homeless for a long time increased slightly, and that’s the group that both sides are fighting over the best way to help them. But yeah, I mean, in a time where housing affordability is one of the biggest issues in the country right now, this is encouraging news nonetheless. “Dreading plans you made yourself? There’s a name for that feeling” Karissa: The next solution is another lifestyle one, and it’s “Dreading plans you made yourself? There’s a name for that feeling.” So you know when you’re the one who made the plans, and then an hour before you’re supposed to leave, you’re on the couch drafting a text reading, “I’m so sorry, something came up,” or, “I feel sick.” There’s actually a name for this experience, and there’s a surprisingly simple trick for getting out the door anyway. Arielle, have you had this feeling before? Arielle: Oh my gosh, this is so relatable. I do find myself kind of dreading plans, and I try not to cancel. I try to push myself through it, but there are some days where I’m just like, “Ooh, I don’t wanna hop on my bike and go through the rain,” and- you know, I don’t wanna see anyone. I don’t wanna talk to anyone. I’m so tired. So yeah, this solution definitely spoke to me. Karissa: And I’m sure probably all of us have been there at some point or another. But this feeling is called anticipatory anxiety. 55% of Gen Z say they feel relief when plans get canceled, and a UK survey found that 68% of under 34s have flaked. But there’s a simple therapist-approved trick to get over this anxiety. Set an alarm for when you need to start getting ready, and when it goes off, shower and get dressed without debating it. So kind of just going forward with it without overthinking it. I think flaking has become so normal now that some people kind of dread planning anything, including their own birthdays and events. And in a time where loneliness is being talked about as a public health issue, canceling plans is a small part of this bigger picture. I feel like it’s kind of a lot easier to cancel plans, too, especially ’cause you don’t even have to call someone to cancel. You just send a text. But usually it’s better for all of us to push through and go forward with that connection anyways. Arielle: I like how this article said that part of the strategy is to imagine a moment when you did push through and you did go to whatever event or whatever gathering or, or meetup that you were once dreading. And chances are you ended up enjoying yourself, and you forgot all about that dread that you had before you actually stepped out the door. And there’s a lot of discussion around protecting our own peace, which I think is valid, but it can make it a lot easier to cop out. We have to be really careful about whether or not we are protecting our peace and we do need that break, because sometimes we definitely do need to take a moment for ourselves, or if we’re just letting the anxiety take over. “Bans cut two forever chemicals by 30 percent in England’s rivers” Karissa: Well, moving on to the next solution, “Bans cut two forever chemicals by 30 percent in England’s rivers.” Two of the most toxic forever chemicals have dropped by almost a third in England’s rivers over the last 10 years, and in fish by about half. The UK basically banned PFOS in 2010 and PFOA in 2020, and the river data now shows the effect, that 30% and 29% drops. But the catch is the chemicals didn’t actually disappear. The total amount is probably the same, but it’s just been diluted and washed out to sea. So it’s still out there, but there’s not as much, you know, going in. There are about 15,000 types of PFAS, and England has just two facilities that can destroy them for good, so not a lot, uh, out there that can get them out of here. PFAS are in the news constantly. They’re in our drinking water, in non-stick pans, rain jackets, and people are increasingly worried about them in their own homes, with good reason of course, because they don’t go away. And the UK government just announced it will start measuring forever chemicals in people’s bodies, so we should have more data on, you know, how exactly forever these chemicals are, and hopefully that will inform more policy in the future. “CAR-T therapy helps stiff person syndrome patients walk and work again” Karissa: The next solution is “CAR-T therapy helps stiff person syndrome patients walk and work again.” Stiff person syndrome is a rare condition that Céline Dion lives with, and until now, there’s been no real treatment for it. Doctors at the Mayo Clinic tried a therapy that’s normally used for cancer, and some patients who needed help walking are now miraculously back at work. CAR-T therapy is something that takes your own immune cells, reprograms them in a lab, and puts them back to wipe out the cells causing the disease. Patients in this one got a single treatment, and one patient, Jonathan, went from needing his family’s help with basic tasks to returning to his favorite hobbies like hunting and fishing again, and he says he hasn’t had a single episode since. This condition, like I mentioned at the beginning, was, you know, kind of brought into the spotlight by Céline Dion’s diagnosis in 2022. She was part of a documentary that brought this condition to the fore. So yeah, CAR-T therapies are one of the biggest stories in medicine right now, and researchers are also trying it out on lupus, MS, and other autoimmune diseases. But as of now, these therapies are incredibly expensive, so it raises the questions about who will have access to them. But hopefully with all medical breakthroughs and advancements, it will become more accessible to more people who need it. “6 hosting habits that leave holiday guests feeling uneasy (and how to avoid them)” Karissa: The last solution I have to share is also a lifestyle-oriented one, and has to do kind of with Thanksgiving and the holidays coming up. “6 hosting habits that leave holiday guests feeling uneasy (and how to avoid them).” So yeah, this holiday party season is about to start, and this one’s all about the stuff your guests notice but would never mention. This goes over a lot of great, uh, you know, pointers about hosting. One prominent one is the parking and coats problem. A party can be beautifully decorated and still feel chaotic if peoples have to circle the block searching for parking, or if they have to hold their jackets for 30 minutes without somewhere to put them. Arielle: The tip that spoke to me was about letting yourself as a host enjoy the gathering as well, instead of always being concerned with, like, cleaning up or prepping things or grabbing whatever, because the people who are there, the people you invited, are there to presumably spend time with you and each other. And it can put people on edge if you’re just constantly, like, fluttering around and, you know, making sure that everything is running perfectly without actually taking the time to settle in. And that, that is kind of challenging for me. Um, especially because I enjoy cleaning. But that’s definitely something that I’m going to be taking to heart this holiday season. And yeah, there’s a lot of other really great tips here as well. But yeah, exciting to get into the festive spirit. Karissa: That’s all the solutions we had this week on The Optimist Daily. Closing quote Arielle: Before we wrap up this episode, we have an inspiring quote, as usual. Karissa: Yes. The quote is, “My turn shall also come: I sense the spreading of a wing.” And that’s from Osip Mandelstam. Very poetic. Yeah, a poetic end to this edition of the weekly roundup. Thanksgiving sign-off Arielle: Yes. We will be back… Oh, we won’t actually be back next week with a full episode, but we will have a special Thanksgiving greeting from The Optimist Daily team to all of you. But in the meantime, Karissa and I wish you all a very, very happy, restful weekend. The post Podcast Transcript November 20th, 2026— A Tourette’s wristband, a trash map and why you dread your plans first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .
