items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News A Sustainable Office Move Is a Business Project: Managing More Than Furniture and Boxes Reading Time: 14 minutes A Sustainable Office Move Is a Business Project: Managing More Than Furniture and Boxes An office move is often described as a logistical exercise involving desks, computers, filing cabinets, and boxes. For businesses, however, changing office locations involves considerably more than transporting physical assets from one building to another. It requires financial planning, operational coordination, employee communication, technology management, and careful attention to business continuity. Every decision, from selecting a moving date to arranging the new workspace, can influence productivity, costs, and the organization’s ability to serve customers. The complexity of an office move becomes particularly evident when multiple departments, technology systems, outside contractors, and building management teams must coordinate their activities. Unlike a typical residential move, an office move frequently involves confidential records, specialized equipment, shared infrastructure, and employees whose daily responsibilities cannot simply be suspended. Delays or mistakes can affect business operations, create unexpected expenses, and disrupt relationships with customers and suppliers. Successful execution therefore depends on treating the move as a structured business project rather than a series of disconnected transportation tasks. Organizations that approach office moving strategically can reduce unnecessary disruption while creating opportunities to improve workplace efficiency and resource allocation. A well-managed move establishes clear responsibilities, realistic schedules, and procedures for identifying potential problems before they interfere with operations. It also considers how the new location will support employees, technology, and future business requirements. Understanding these interconnected responsibilities is essential for companies planning an office move, whether they operate a small professional practice or a larger organization with multiple departments. Office Moving Requires Strategic Business Planning An office move should begin with a clear understanding of why the business needs a different workspace. Some organizations move because they have outgrown their existing facilities, while others seek more efficient layouts, better access to employees and customers, or lower long-term occupancy costs. Changes in workforce size, hybrid working arrangements, and operational requirements can also influence the decision. Before committing to a new location, business leaders should evaluate how the proposed move supports broader organizational objectives. Without this assessment, a company may successfully transfer its belongings while failing to address the underlying problems that prompted the move. Strategic planning also requires establishing a realistic timeline that accounts for the organization’s operational requirements. Lease expiration dates, renovation schedules, technology installation, vendor availability, and employee workloads can create dependencies that are easy to underestimate. A company that schedules its move before essential infrastructure is ready may experience unnecessary downtime or incur expenses associated with temporary arrangements. Project managers should identify significant milestones, assign responsible personnel, and establish contingency plans for delays. Treating each activity as part of an integrated schedule provides management with greater visibility into progress and allows potential conflicts to be addressed before they become operational problems. For businesses operating in metropolitan markets, office moving can involve additional considerations related to building access, traffic conditions, parking restrictions, and coordination with property managers. Greater Boston, including communities such as Newton, Cambridge, Woburn, and Brookline, presents a variety of commercial environments, from established office buildings to mixed-use properties with limited loading access. Businesses must consider how these physical conditions affect moving schedules, equipment requirements, and the safe handling of office assets. Engaging an experienced moving company early can help organizations evaluate practical challenges that might otherwise be overlooked. The broader objective is to ensure that the moving process supports business priorities rather than creating avoidable interruptions. Coordinating Professional Moving Services and External Partners The selection and coordination of outside service providers can materially influence the success of an office move. Professional movers, information technology specialists, building managers, furniture installers, and cleaning contractors may all be involved at different stages, creating potential scheduling conflicts and overlapping responsibilities. These concerns are particularly relevant in commercial markets such as Boston, Cambridge, and Newton, where office buildings may have different loading facilities, elevator procedures, and access restrictions. Businesses must therefore establish clear expectations regarding scheduling, equipment handling, property access, and communication before work begins. Written responsibilities and coordinated schedules can help prevent one contractor’s delay from disrupting several others. These logistical requirements become more significant when businesses move between commercial properties across Greater Boston. Office moves involving communities such as Brookline and Somerville may require coordination between different building management teams, loading arrangements, and designated moving hours. Professional moving services can help organizations manage packing, transportation, and temporary storage while accommodating these property-specific requirements. Piece by Piece Movers , a professional moving and storage company serving Greater Boston since 2008, operates in this environment with services for residential and commercial customers. Its comprehensive moving services provide practical support for packing, transportation, and storage needs, while its specialized commercial moving services help businesses coordinate office moves, protect valuable equipment, and manage complex moving requirements. The company’s emphasis on careful handling, property protection, and detailed coordination reflects important considerations when evaluating moving providers. Vendor management should continue throughout the planning and execution process rather than ending once service agreements have been signed. Businesses should confirm which party is responsible for packing particular items, disconnecting equipment, protecting common areas, and placing furniture at the destination. Insurance arrangements, service limitations, building access requirements, and procedures for reporting damage should also be understood in advance. Regular communication between internal project leaders and external providers can help identify scheduling conflicts and reduce uncertainty as moving dates approach. Assigning clear points of contact also allows unexpected issues to be addressed promptly. When responsibilities are documented and schedules remain coordinated, employees can stay focused on their work while specialized moving tasks are handled by the appropriate professionals. Building a Realistic Budget for the Entire Office Move Office moving expenses extend well beyond the price of transporting furniture, equipment, and supplies. Businesses may need to account for security deposits, lease-related obligations, utility connections, network installation, furniture purchases , temporary storage, and changes to the new workspace. Some costs are immediately visible, while others emerge through operational interruptions, employee overtime, or unexpected building requirements. A company that budgets only for transportation may underestimate the total financial commitment associated with changing locations. Developing a comprehensive budget is therefore an essential part of responsible project management. A useful financial plan separates predictable expenses from costs that depend on changing circumstances. Fixed expenses may include contracted moving services, approved furniture purchases, and agreed installation charges, while variable costs may arise from additional packing materials, schedule changes, or unforeseen building limitations. Management should request detailed estimates and clarify which services are included before comparing vendor proposals. The lowest initial quotation may not represent the lowest overall cost if important tasks require separate arrangements or additional charges. A contingency reserve can provide flexibility when unexpected conditions affect the moving schedule or operational requirements. Businesses should also consider the financial consequences of productivity losses during the transition. Even a relatively short interruption can affect organizations that depend on client appointments, continuous customer support, order processing, or time-sensitive professional services. These indirect costs may be difficult to calculate precisely, but ignoring them can produce an incomplete financial picture. Companies can limit exposure by planning critical activities outside peak operating periods and maintaining essential services during the transition. Evaluating direct costs alongside operational risks helps management make better-informed decisions about timing, staffing, and the resources required for a successful office move. Protecting Business Continuity During the Transition Business continuity is among the most important considerations in an office move because customers and commercial obligations rarely disappear while a company changes locations. Employees may need access to shared files, communication platforms, inventory systems, and specialized equipment even when parts of the workplace are temporarily unavailable. A poorly coordinated move can interrupt these functions, causing missed deadlines and reduced service quality. Business leaders should identify which activities must remain operational and determine how those activities will be supported throughout the moving period. This assessment helps distinguish essential services from tasks that can be temporarily suspended without serious consequences. A phased moving strategy can be appropriate for businesses that cannot tolerate a complete operational shutdown. Rather than transferring every department simultaneously, an organization may move selected teams or equipment in stages while maintaining critical functions at the original location. This approach can reduce disruption, although it may also increase coordination requirements and introduce additional costs. Other companies may benefit from scheduling physical moving activities during weekends or other periods of reduced demand. The appropriate strategy depends on the organization’s size, industry, customer obligations, and ability to operate across multiple locations during the transition. Continuity planning should also address the possibility that some activities will not proceed according to schedule. Internet installation delays, missing equipment, unavailable workstations, or unexpected building restrictions can interfere with the planned reopening of an office. Management should establish backup communication arrangements, alternative work locations where feasible, and procedures for handling urgent customer needs. Employees should understand whom to contact when systems or facilities are temporarily unavailable. A structured continuity plan cannot eliminate every disruption, but it can reduce the likelihood that an isolated problem develops into a broader business interruption. Managing Technology, Data Security, and IT Infrastructure Modern offices depend heavily on technology, making information systems one of the most sensitive components of a business move. Computers, servers, networking equipment, communication devices, printers, and specialized electronic systems may need to be disconnected, transported, reinstalled, and tested. Improper handling or incomplete preparation can result in equipment damage, data access problems, or extended downtime. Information technology personnel should therefore participate in planning from the earliest stages rather than becoming involved immediately before moving day. Their responsibilities may include documenting existing infrastructure, identifying dependencies, and confirming that the new location can support required systems. Data security introduces additional responsibilities that are not present in many other types of moving projects. Businesses may maintain confidential customer records, financial information, employee data, proprietary documents, and regulated information that must remain protected throughout the transition. Physical records should be inventoried and transported using appropriate security procedures, while electronic systems should be backed up and protected against unauthorized access. Organizations may also need to consider contractual obligations and applicable privacy or industry requirements when transferring sensitive materials. Clear custody procedures, restricted access, and documented responsibilities can help reduce the possibility of misplaced information or security breaches. Technology planning should extend beyond successful transportation to include full operational testing at the new office. Network connectivity, wireless coverage, telephone systems, printers, conference equipment, and security controls should be verified before employees are expected to resume normal work. Businesses should also confirm that internet connections and other essential services are active when required, rather than assuming that installation appointments guarantee immediate functionality. Testing should involve employees who regularly use specialized software or equipment because technical readiness does not always translate into practical usability. A systematic verification process helps identify problems before they affect customers, deadlines, or routine business activities. Employee Communication and Workforce Coordination Employees are directly affected by office moving decisions, yet their needs can receive less attention than equipment, budgets, and transportation schedules. A change of workplace may influence commuting arrangements, parking availability, daily routines, collaboration patterns, and access to essential facilities. Even when a new office offers improved working conditions, uncertainty about the transition can create frustration and distract employees from their responsibilities. Management should communicate the reasons for the move, the expected schedule, and the practical changes employees will experience. Clear information helps reduce speculation and allows staff members to make necessary personal and professional arrangements. Communication should be organized around specific responsibilities rather than limited to broad company announcements. Employees may need instructions for packing personal belongings, labeling assigned equipment, clearing workstations, and handling documents that should not be transported with ordinary office supplies. Department managers should identify specialized requirements and communicate them to the central project team. Businesses can also designate representatives from different departments to provide feedback and report potential problems. This approach creates a more complete understanding of operational needs while reducing the possibility that important tasks are overlooked. The first days in a new workplace can be particularly challenging if employees lack guidance about their surroundings or access to essential resources. Orientation materials can explain workstation assignments, meeting room locations, security procedures, parking arrangements, and available shared facilities. Employees should also know how to report missing equipment, technology problems, or other issues that arise during the transition. Encouraging feedback helps management identify problems that may not have been apparent during planning. An office move becomes easier to manage when employees understand both the practical steps involved and the role they play in restoring normal operations. Inventory Management and the Protection of Business Assets A detailed inventory provides the foundation for an organized office move because it establishes what must be transferred, stored, replaced, or discarded. Offices often accumulate furniture, electronic equipment, paper records, supplies, and miscellaneous items over many years. Moving everything without first assessing its usefulness can increase transportation costs and create unnecessary clutter in the new workspace. Businesses should review their assets before packing begins and determine which items remain necessary for current operations. This process can also reveal opportunities to standardize equipment, remove obsolete materials, and avoid purchasing replacements for items that are already available. An effective inventory system should record important information about valuable or operationally significant assets. Equipment descriptions, asset identification numbers, assigned departments, destination locations, and handling requirements can help maintain accountability throughout the move. Labels should be consistent and sufficiently clear to support both transportation and unpacking. High-value items and specialized equipment may require additional documentation, protective packaging, or handling procedures. When the inventory is coordinated with the new office layout, moving teams can place items more accurately and reduce the need for repeated internal transportation after delivery. Asset management also includes decisions about disposal, donation, recycling, and temporary storage. Furniture that no longer suits the organization’s requirements may be more expensive to transport and retain than to replace, although replacement decisions should account for purchasing and environmental costs. Electronic devices may require secure data removal before disposal or recycling, particularly when they contain confidential business information. Items that will not be immediately needed at the new location may require organized storage with appropriate access and tracking arrangements. Making these decisions before moving day reduces congestion, simplifies logistics, and supports more efficient use of the new workspace. Incorporating Sustainability and Environmental Responsibility Changing office locations presents a significant opportunity to reduce an organization’s environmental footprint while reinforcing corporate responsibility goals. Commercial relocations frequently generate substantial waste through discarded furniture, obsolete electronics, single-use packing materials, and unnecessary transportation trips. Treating sustainability as a core project requirement rather than an afterthought allows businesses to minimize landfill contributions and often reduce disposal and purchasing expenses. By evaluating environmental impacts alongside cost and operational efficiency, companies can align their physical transition with broader sustainability commitments. Responsible resource management begins well before packing materials are ordered. Instead of relying exclusively on disposable cardboard boxes and plastic wrap, organizations can work with moving providers that offer reusable plastic crates, padded blankets, and recyclable packing supplies. Furniture and fixtures that no longer fit the new floor plan can be evaluated for refurbishment, internal reuse, donation to local nonprofits, or resale through commercial liquidators. When electronic equipment reaches the end of its useful life, partnering with certified e-waste recyclers ensures that hazardous materials are handled safely and valuable components are recovered without compromising data security. Sustainability considerations should also extend to transportation logistics and the setup of the destination workspace. Consolidating shipments, selecting energy-efficient moving fleets, and scheduling deliveries during off-peak traffic hours can help lower fuel consumption and emissions. Once inside the new office, businesses can prioritize energy-efficient lighting, smart climate controls, responsibly sourced furnishings, and accessible recycling and composting stations. Embedding these practices into the relocation plan ensures that the new workplace operates more efficiently while demonstrating a tangible commitment to environmental stewardship for employees, clients, and stakeholders. Understanding Building Access and Moving Logistics Commercial buildings can introduce logistical requirements that differ substantially from those associated with moving between private residences. Property managers may restrict moving activities to designated hours, require advance elevator reservations, or establish rules for protecting floors, walls, and common areas. Loading docks may have limited capacity, while parking restrictions can complicate vehicle access and equipment transportation. Businesses should obtain relevant building policies from both the existing and destination properties early in the planning process. Failure to coordinate these arrangements can result in delays even when the moving team and equipment are otherwise ready. Physical access should be evaluated in detail before the move begins. Doorway dimensions, elevator capacities, stairwell configurations, loading routes, and furniture sizes can influence how equipment is packed and transported. Large conference tables, modular workstations, filing systems, and specialized machinery may require disassembly or particular handling arrangements. A site assessment can help identify obstacles that would be difficult to resolve once moving activities are underway. It can also support more accurate estimates by clarifying the labor, equipment, and time required for the project. Logistical coordination becomes particularly important in densely developed commercial areas where multiple businesses share limited transportation and loading infrastructure. Traffic conditions, local parking rules, building security procedures, and the availability of freight elevators may affect the sequence of moving activities. Project managers should confirm these details with property representatives and service providers rather than relying on assumptions based on ordinary building access. The moving schedule should include enough flexibility to address minor interruptions without disrupting every subsequent activity. Thorough logistical preparation helps protect business assets, reduce unnecessary handling, and maintain a more predictable moving process. Designing the New Office for Operational Efficiency An office move provides an opportunity to evaluate whether the existing workplace arrangement still supports the organization’s needs. Businesses may have changed their staffing levels, departmental structures, technology requirements, or working practices since their previous office was established. Simply reproducing the old layout at a new address can preserve inefficiencies that originally contributed to the need for additional space. Management should examine how employees use workstations, meeting rooms, storage areas, and shared facilities before finalizing the new arrangement. The objective is to align the physical environment with actual operating requirements rather than base decisions solely on appearance or available floor area. Workspace planning should account for collaboration, concentration, accessibility, and the practical movement of people and materials. Departments that communicate frequently may benefit from appropriate proximity, while employees responsible for confidential work may require quieter or more private spaces. Meeting facilities should reflect realistic usage patterns, and storage should be located where employees can access necessary materials without disrupting other activities. Electrical outlets, network connections, lighting, and ergonomic considerations should be incorporated into the layout before furniture is installed. Addressing these requirements early reduces the cost and inconvenience of making substantial adjustments after employees begin using the office. The design process should also consider future flexibility because business requirements can change faster than commercial leases or furniture replacement cycles. Modular furnishings, adaptable meeting spaces, and carefully planned technology infrastructure may allow organizations to accommodate workforce changes without another major reconfiguration. Companies should avoid assuming that current headcount or working arrangements will remain unchanged throughout their occupancy. However, flexibility must be weighed against cost, available space, and the specific needs of the organization. A well-planned office supports present operations while providing reasonable capacity to respond to future business developments. Risk Management and Contingency Planning Every office move involves uncertainty, even when the project has been carefully planned. Equipment may be damaged, vendors may encounter delays, building access may change, or essential services may not be available as expected. These problems become more consequential when several project activities depend on one another. A business should identify significant risks before moving begins and assess their potential effects on cost, safety, scheduling, and continuity. This process allows management to direct attention toward issues that could have the greatest operational consequences. Risk management should include practical measures for reducing both the likelihood and impact of foreseeable problems. Protective packing, accurate labeling, documented asset inventories, and suitable handling arrangements can help limit physical damage. Confirmed vendor schedules, alternative communication systems, and pre-move technology testing can reduce the risk of operational interruption. Insurance coverage should also be reviewed so that management understands applicable terms, exclusions, and claim procedures. Although no arrangement can guarantee a problem-free move, preparation creates a more controlled environment in which unexpected events can be addressed promptly. Contingency planning becomes useful when a project encounters circumstances that cannot be resolved immediately. If the destination office is not ready, a company may need temporary storage, alternative work arrangements, or a revised sequence for moving departments. If important technology is unavailable, managers may need to activate backup systems or adjust customer service procedures. These responses should be considered before the scheduled move rather than developed entirely during a crisis. Assigning decision-making authority in advance allows the organization to respond more quickly while maintaining clear accountability for costs and operational consequences. Measuring the Success of an Office Move The completion of physical transportation does not necessarily mean that an office move has been successful. A business may have delivered all its furniture and equipment to the new location while still experiencing unresolved technology problems, employee confusion, or operational delays. Project evaluation should therefore consider outcomes beyond whether moving vehicles arrived on schedule. Relevant measures may include total project costs, the duration of downtime, asset condition, employee readiness, and the restoration of essential services. These indicators provide a more complete picture of whether the move achieved its operational objectives. A structured post-move review helps organizations identify outstanding tasks and resolve problems systematically. Management should confirm that equipment inventories are accurate, employee workstations are functional, building access arrangements are complete, and service providers have fulfilled their agreed responsibilities. Departments may also need time to test routine workflows and determine whether the new layout supports their daily activities. Employee feedback can reveal issues involving accessibility, communication, storage, or technology that were not obvious during initial inspections. Documenting these findings allows management to prioritize corrective action and avoid leaving smaller problems unresolved indefinitely. The lessons from an office move can also inform future facilities decisions and broader project management practices. Companies may discover weaknesses in vendor coordination, internal communication, purchasing procedures, or contingency planning that extend beyond moving activities. Reviewing these issues can improve organizational readiness for office expansions, renovations, departmental changes, or other complex operational projects. Management should distinguish temporary adjustment difficulties from persistent problems that require substantial intervention. Ultimately, the strongest measure of success is whether the new workplace enables employees and business systems to function effectively while delivering the intended operational and financial benefits. Treating an Office Move as a Business Investment An office move is far more than the physical transfer of desks, equipment, and supplies. It is a business project that connects strategic planning, financial management, technology infrastructure, workforce coordination, and operational risk. Each of these responsibilities influences the others, making it difficult to achieve a successful outcome through transportation planning alone. Organizations that recognize this complexity are better positioned to establish realistic schedules, coordinate the necessary professionals, and protect essential business activities. The quality of preparation often determines how effectively the company can continue operating during and after the transition. The most effective approach combines clear leadership with detailed execution. Business managers should establish objectives, assign responsibilities, develop comprehensive budgets, and communicate consistently with employees and external providers. Technology readiness, asset protection, building access, and contingency procedures should receive the same attention as the physical movement of office furniture. These measures help reduce uncertainty and create a structured process for addressing challenges as they arise. They also allow businesses to evaluate the move according to its wider operational consequences rather than simply the immediate cost of transportation. A carefully managed office move can create lasting value when the new workspace improves efficiency, supports employees, and aligns with the organization’s long-term goals. Achieving these benefits requires decisions that extend well beyond moving day, including how the workplace is configured, how systems are restored, and how employees adapt to their new environment. Businesses that treat office moving as a coordinated investment rather than an isolated logistical expense can make better use of their resources and reduce preventable disruption. The central principle is straightforward: moving an office involves transporting physical assets, but successfully managing the move means protecting the business that depends on them. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Smarter Infrastructure Planning Can Reduce the Environmental Impact of Data Centers Reading Time: 4 minutes How Smarter Infrastructure Planning Can Reduce the Environmental Impact of Data Centers The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and digital services is creating growing demand for data centers. While these facilities support essential technologies, their development also raises important environmental questions. Data centers require substantial electricity, construction materials, cooling infrastructure, and specialized equipment. Their environmental footprint begins long before the first server becomes operational. Construction activities, transportation requirements, material selection, and equipment installation can all contribute to emissions and resource consumption. As developers face increasing pressure to balance digital growth with environmental responsibility, infrastructure planning is becoming an important part of the conversation. Reducing environmental impacts requires looking beyond operational energy efficiency and considering how facilities are designed, constructed, and maintained throughout their lifecycles. Sustainable Data Center Development Begins With Better Planning Data centers’ environmental performance depends on decisions made throughout development and operation. Site selection, building design, electricity availability, cooling requirements, and construction methods can all influence resource consumption. For example, developing a facility in a location with suitable electrical infrastructure may reduce the need for certain additional construction activities. Similarly, designing equipment layouts for efficient installation and maintenance access can help avoid unnecessary later modifications. However, sustainable development involves balancing several considerations. A location with favorable electricity conditions may still face challenges related to water availability, land use, or transportation access. Developers must therefore evaluate environmental factors together rather than focusing exclusively on a single performance measure. Early planning provides opportunities to identify these trade-offs before major financial and construction commitments are made. Energy Efficiency Remains Central to Environmental Performance Electricity consumption is one of the most significant environmental considerations associated with data center operations. Computing equipment requires continuous power, while cooling and supporting systems contribute to overall energy demand. Improving efficiency can reduce the electricity needed to deliver a given level of computing performance. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s ENERGY STAR guidance for data centers provides resources related to measuring and improving data center energy performance. Energy management begins with understanding how a facility consumes electricity. Developers and operators can evaluate cooling efficiency, power distribution losses, equipment utilization, and monitoring systems. However, energy efficiency should not be confused with eliminating environmental impacts. A facility can become more efficient while its total electricity consumption increases because of additional computing capacity. For this reason, sustainability assessments should consider both operational efficiency and overall resource demand. Equipment Logistics Can Influence Construction-Related Emissions Building a data center requires transporting and installing large electrical and mechanical components. Transformers, backup generators, cooling systems, and other specialized equipment may travel considerable distances before reaching their final locations. Transportation requirements can involve heavy-duty vehicles, specialized trailers, cranes, and additional handling equipment. Industrial logistics providers such as prolift rigging operate within this environment, where the movement and positioning of heavy machinery must be coordinated with construction activities. Although specialized transportation cannot always be avoided, better logistics planning can help reduce unnecessary movements. For example, coordinating equipment deliveries with installation schedules may limit repeated transportation between storage facilities and construction sites. Preparing suitable access routes can also reduce the need for additional handling or temporary relocation. These measures can support operational efficiency while potentially reducing fuel consumption and associated emissions. However, environmental benefits depend on actual project conditions, transportation distances, equipment choices, and the number of movements avoided. Measuring these factors is important when evaluating whether a logistics strategy delivers meaningful environmental improvements. Construction Materials Have Environmental Impacts Beyond the Building Site Data center development involves substantial quantities of concrete, steel, electrical equipment, and mechanical infrastructure. Producing these materials requires energy and raw resources, creating environmental impacts before construction begins. Material transportation, installation, maintenance, and eventual disposal also contribute to a facility’s lifecycle footprint. The World Green Building Council’s resources on embodied carbon explain why emissions associated with building materials and construction processes deserve attention alongside operational energy consumption. For developers, this creates opportunities to evaluate material choices and construction methods. Using appropriate quantities of materials, reducing avoidable waste, and considering the durability of major components can support more responsible construction. However, selecting materials solely based on their initial environmental impact may overlook other important factors. Durability, maintenance requirements, structural performance, and replacement frequency can influence environmental outcomes over time. A lifecycle perspective helps developers understand these trade-offs. Cooling Systems Require Careful Resource Management Cooling is essential to maintaining reliable data center operations. Computing equipment generates heat, and facilities must remove that heat to maintain suitable operating conditions. Different cooling technologies require different levels of electricity, water, mechanical equipment, and maintenance. Air-based cooling, evaporative cooling, and liquid cooling systems each present advantages and limitations depending on facility design and local conditions. Water availability is particularly important in regions where resources are already under pressure. A cooling strategy that reduces electricity consumption may increase water use, creating a trade-off that developers need to evaluate. Climate, computing density, equipment requirements, and local infrastructure should all influence cooling decisions. Rather than assuming one technology is universally more sustainable, developers should assess each option’s environmental consequences for the specific project. Designing for Maintenance Can Reduce Future Resource Waste Sustainable infrastructure planning should consider what happens after construction. Data centers require regular maintenance, equipment upgrades, and occasional replacement of major components. Poor equipment access can make these activities more difficult and may require additional construction work. For example, replacing a large cooling unit could require unnecessary demolition or structural modifications if the original design did not account for access. Providing suitable maintenance routes, equipment clearances, and replacement strategies can reduce these complications. Modular infrastructure may also offer advantages in some applications by allowing teams to replace or expand individual components without extensive changes to surrounding systems. However, modular designs are not automatically more sustainable. Their environmental performance depends on material use, manufacturing processes, operational efficiency, and expected service life. The goal is to develop facilities that can adapt to changing requirements without creating avoidable waste. Sustainable Growth Requires a Broader Infrastructure Perspective The environmental challenges associated with data center expansion cannot be addressed through a single technology or construction practice. Energy consumption, water use, material production, transportation, and equipment maintenance all contribute to the broader environmental picture. Developers can make more informed decisions by evaluating these factors throughout the project lifecycle. Early design coordination, efficient equipment logistics, responsible material selection, and long-term maintenance planning can help identify opportunities to reduce unnecessary resource consumption. These strategies do not eliminate the environmental footprint of digital infrastructure. However, they can support a more deliberate approach to managing its impacts. As demand for computing capacity continues to grow, responsible infrastructure development will require balancing technological progress with environmental considerations. The challenge is not simply building more data centers. It is understanding how each stage of development can contribute to a more resource-conscious digital economy. items.descriptionOriginal: If you’re sitting down for seafood, should you order the farmed or wild-caught fish? In this day of over-exploited seas, the farmed fillet might seem like a better choice. And yet, in many cases, those farmed salmon or trout also contribute to over-fishing , because they’re raised on diets of wild-caught sardines, herring, anchovies, or mackerel . But researchers have now developed a potential solution to this problem: a meat-free, algal diet that farmed fish can thrive on. As human populations expand, farmed fish are becoming an increasing protein source. Roughly 100 million tons of farmed fish and crustaceans are harvested worldwide each year. In order to feed them, at least 20 millions of wild-caught fish are processed into fishmeal and fish oil each year—most of it consumed by farmed predatory species such as salmon and trout. But even non-predatory farmed fish like tilapia have hidden costs, because they’re often raised on cornmeal or soy, requiring agricultural land that might otherwise feed humans directly. A team of researchers at the University of California Santa Cruz has spent years developing fish feeds based on two types of marine algae, called Nannochloropsis and Schizochytrium , which are also being used or studied as sources for biofuels, farm animal feed , and nutritional additives for human foods. In 2020, the team showed that farmed tilapia grew normally on blends of these two algae . In the new study, published October 16 in Antioxidants , they tried feeding these algal blends to a commonly farmed carnivorous fish, rainbow trout. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby Fish on the algal diet also had similar levels of polyunsaturated fatty acids, including omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (which are considered important for preventing chronic disease in humans). items.descriptionOriginal: At the height of a Saturday dinner rush in Singapore, a coffee shop server named Lau Guat Toh spotted an unattended bag and did what came naturally to her - she protected it, placed it under a security camera, and waited. Inside was $20,000 in cash, enough to rattle most people, but Lau and her colleagues "did not dare touch" it, a detail that says more about their character than any declaration of honesty could. The bag's owner, a noodle manufacturer who had rushed off to a friend's wake, returned at 11pm simply trying his luck, and found everything intact. What lingers in the story is the quiet ecosystem of goodness surrounding the moment: a boss who had spent his evening delivering donated soup to elderly residents, a customer whose first response to losing a fortune was not panic but acceptance, and a server who plans to keep her $200 reward as a souvenir rather than spend it. "If something is meant to come, it will come," said the man who lost the money - and somehow, in this small coffee shop in Bedok, it did.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The best holiday parties tend to be the ones where nobody thinks about the hosting at all. Guests walk in, find a spot for their coat, settle in with a plate and a drink, and the evening carries them along. When something’s slightly off, though, they feel it long before they’d ever say it out loud. A guest who can’t hear the person next to them, or who’s stuck eating bread rolls all night because everything else has nuts in it, probably won’t complain. They’ll just leave a little earlier than they planned. The good news is that most of these little snags are easy to catch if you picture the evening from your guests’ side of the door. So let’s walk through it the way they will, from the moment they pull up to the moment they say goodbye. Before holiday guests arrive A clean home where it counts First impressions start at the entryway. Clutter underfoot or a sink full of dishes can make guests more focused on where to step than on catching up with each other. You don’t need a spotless house, though. Rooms that will stay closed can wait. Put your energy into the spaces people will use, like the bathroom, kitchen, and living room, plus the guest room if anyone’s staying over. Spreading the cleaning across a few days instead of saving it all for the night before keeps you from running on fumes when the doorbell rings. Parking, coats and the weather Even a beautifully decorated party can feel disorganized if guests circle the block looking for a parking spot or end up holding their coats for the first half hour. A short message a few days ahead covering where to park and what to expect when they arrive takes the guesswork out of it. If you live somewhere with snow or ice, it helps to have a backup plan ready in case the weather turns on the day. Food everyone can eat Nobody wants to be the guest pushing food around a plate because of an allergy the host didn’t know about. Before you settle on a menu, send a quick note asking whether anyone has dietary needs. Even if no one replies with anything, having a few dishes that happen to be gluten-free, vegan, or nut-free is an easy way to make sure no one goes hungry. Making holiday guests comfortable once the party starts Room to move around Every home has its own quirks, and the layout shapes how comfortable people feel once they’re inside. Before the party, take a slow lap through your space as if you’d never seen it. Where will people gather? Is the buffet in a spot that blocks the hallway? Is there somewhere to sit near the food? Shumaila Panhwar , a hosting professional, recommends exactly that kind of walkthrough. “When you walk through the space from the perspective of the guests and their experience, it makes it easier to determine placement of items and what makes sense best for flow,” she advises. Music that stays in the background A festive playlist does wonders for the mood, right up until people have to lean in and shout to hear each other. Keep the volume low enough that conversation comes first. Your neighbors will appreciate it too, and nothing ends a party faster than a noise complaint. Being a present host Let yourself enjoy it Here’s the one that catches even the most organized hosts. It’s easy to spend the whole evening refilling bowls and checking the oven, but your guests came to see you. Your presence matters most when people are meeting for the first time and could use an introduction to get a conversation going. Making a plan the night before and running through it once can help a lot. When you know everything is ready, it gets easier to set down the serving spoon, pour yourself a glass of something, and join the people you invited, which, when you think about it, is what made you want to host in the first place. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A cell therapy built to fight cancer is helping people with stiff person syndrome get back on their feet. In an early trial led by neurologists at Mayo Clinic, patients who had needed family members to help them walk and handle daily tasks regained enough function to return to work, exercise, and hobbies after a single round of CAR-T cell therapy. The results, published in JAMA Neurology , point to a treatment that targets the root of the disease instead of only easing its symptoms. A rare disease with no cure What stiff person syndrome does to the body Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the central nervous system. The result can be severe rigidity throughout the body, painful muscle spasms, and frequent falls. Decades of research have produced treatments that can soften symptoms, but none that cure it. The condition drew global attention in December 2022, when singer Céline Dion revealed her diagnosis . In an Instagram video, she said it affected “every aspect of my daily life,” including her ability to sing. How CAR-T works against stiff person syndrome CAR-T therapy is already an established treatment for some blood cancers. Doctors extract a patient’s T cells, a type of immune cell, and engineer them in a lab to seek out and destroy specific targets. For this trial, the cells were redesigned to eliminate the immune cells that drive SPS, using a CD19-targeted therapy called mivocabtagene autoleucel. Each participant received a single treatment, and the study ran across three sites, Mayo Clinic among them. Dr. Anastasia Zekeridou , a neurologist and researcher at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, said the scale of the response stood out. “What was most striking was the degree of improvement we saw in some patients,” she said. “With existing treatments, we may be able to improve symptoms but we very rarely see patients return to their previous level of function.” Patients back at work and on the treadmill Jonathan Walden: hunting and fishing again Before the trial, Jonathan Walden relied on his family for help with walking and basic daily tasks. He has since returned to his job. “I can go to work every single day. I can do everything I did before. I go hunting; I can go fishing,” he said. “I have not had one episode since receiving treatment.” Shari St. Germain: seven minutes on a treadmill Shari St. Germain’s illness progressed from severe leg cramps and trouble walking to rigid muscles and falls. After CAR-T, she said, each day has felt “better and better.” One morning she felt well enough to try the treadmill. “My husband comes running in because I’m crying and he’s like: ‘Are you OK?’ And I’m like: ‘I just walked for seven minutes on the treadmill,'” she said. Next questions for CAR-T in neurology Will the improvements last? The researchers are clear that this is early evidence from a small, nonrandomized trial, and that larger studies are needed. “These early results are very encouraging and the key question now is whether those improvements will be sustained over time,” Zekeridou said. Beyond blood cancer Dr. Sean Pittock, who chairs the department of neurology at Mayo Clinic, sees a wider opening. “CAR-T therapy has already transformed the treatment of some cancers, and we are now beginning to see its potential in autoimmune neurologic diseases,” he said, adding that the results offer hope for other immune-mediated neurologic conditions with few effective options. Yasmin Sheikh, head of policy and public affairs at the UK blood cancer charity Anthony Nolan, which was not involved in the trial, called the research “an exciting development” and more evidence that CAR-T could reach well beyond blood cancer. If the gains hold in larger trials, people with stiff person syndrome could have something they have never had before: a treatment aimed at giving them back the lives the disease took, not just making those lives easier to manage. items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have long used chemogenetics to study brains in the lab. A pilot trial for seizures is its first leap into medicine. Flashing lights. Buzzing noises. A sudden wave of fear. For some people with epilepsy, these sensations herald an oncoming seizure. Drugs can keep some seizures at bay, but over 30 percent of patients don’t respond to them, a statistic that hasn’t budged in decades. Frequent, uncontrolled seizures rob people of a normal life. They can’t drive or swim alone. Some struggle to stay in school, hold down jobs, or maintain relationships. And despite growing public awareness, stigma lingers. For people with severe drug-resistant epilepsy, surgery is an option. If the seizures are associated with a local brain region, doctors can remove the tissue. It’s a drastic operation, but it isn’t rare. In 2024, over 2,000 patients elected to undergo the procedure. Depending on the brain region removed, surgery can control seizures in nearly 70 percent of patients, but they risk losing memory, language, and other cognitive abilities. A new gene therapy could offer an alternative. In a clinical trial , three men who had lived with epilepsy for at least a decade saw monthly seizures drop over 90 percent. One remained seizure-free for a year. In the trial, the team shuttled a gene into a small patch of the hippocampus, the source of their seizures. The gene produces a kind of protein “dimmer switch” in neurons. Normally silent, the protein springs into action when activated by an FDA-approved drug, allowing scientists to dial down the region’s electrical activity rather than shutting it off completely—something that’s not possible with current treatments. The technology, called chemogenetics, has been a staple of animal research in neuroscience. The findings, though early, suggest it could finally make the leap into human medicine. “It certainly has caused a lot of excitement in the field,” said Dimitri Kullmann at University College London to Chemical & Engineering News , who was not involved in the study. Chemical Romance Intricate webs of neurons underlie every brain function. Our ability to feel, move, remember, and reason all stem from electrical and chemical signals that wire brain cells into circuits. It’s a delicate balance. Some neurons release chemicals that fire up their neighbors; others dampen them. In epilepsy, this goes awry. The causes are plenty. Genetic mutations can disrupt how neurons develop or function. Brain injuries, tumors, stroke, and infections can also fuel the condition. In some frustrating cases, the culprit remains unknown. Rebalancing these circuits could tame runaway seizures. Most antiseizure drugs prevent neurons from firing too rapidly or boosting inhibitory chemical signals. But medication is a Band-Aid, not a cure. Because the drugs flood the whole brain, they can trigger fatigue, dizziness, mood swings, and sometimes more serious side effects , including liver or heart problems. Dampening electrical activity at the source could be a better bet. Around two decades ago, an emerging technology called chemogenetics first amazed neuroscientists with its precise control of single neurons. The technology relies on two parts: gene therapy and a drug. First, an engineered virus delivers a gene encoding a designer receptor into targeted neurons. The receptor is silent until a specific drug activates it. By adjusting the drug’s dose, scientists can fine tune the activity of modified neurons. Rather than simply flicking neurons on or off, the approach is flexible and targeted. Chemogenetics soon caught the attention of epilepsy researchers. In 2019, a team at Ghent University in Belgium tested the method in mice with seizures originating in the hippocampus. They delivered a designer receptor called hMADi to the region. A single dose of clozapine, an FDA-approved antipsychotic, controlled seizures for at least 15 hours. With repeated treatment, seizures nearly vanished. A subsequent study in monkeys also dramatically slashed seizures. Given these encouraging findings, some researchers were ready to take the next step. “I think scientists like me felt like, ‘Why haven’t we tried it in humans yet?’” said study author Minmin Luo at the Chinese Institute for Brain Research. Restoring Balance The trial enrolled three men under 40 diagnosed with epilepsy for 10 to 25 years. All had tried at least two antiseizure medications without success. Brain scans traced their seizures to a scarred hippocampus on one side of the brain. The same structure on the other side remained healthy. Despite their long history of epilepsy, none showed notable signs of cognitive troubles. Similar to previous work, the team delivered a gene encoding the hMADi receptor into the damaged region of each patient’s hippocampus in a series of three shots. A dye mixed with the therapy confirmed it reached nearly the entire region in two patients and spread slightly beyond it in the third. The infusion took roughly two hours. Two weeks later, the men began taking clozapine pills every eight hours. After five months, their average monthly seizure count had dropped from roughly four to nearly zero. Brain recordings also showed far fewer epilepsy-related electrical spikes, and their damaged hippocampuses increased metabolism, though levels remained below those in the region’s healthy counterpart. The benefits lasted. In check-ups throughout the following year, two patients remained seizure-free. The third experienced two “breakthrough” seizures after an unexpected interruption in medication, but the seizures stopped once he restarted the drug regime. All three participants also reported improved quality of life. The study’s main goal, however, was to gauge safety. The viral carrier has a relatively established safety record, but high doses have been linked to severe immune reactions and even deaths . Delivering the therapy directly into brain tissue requires far smaller doses than when injected into the bloodstream and perhaps, counterintuitively, could be safer overall. Blood tests, brain scans, and other assessments find no major side effects. One patient experienced a temporary rise in liver enzymes, a sign of liver stress, but levels returned to normal without intervention. The team plans to expand the trial, but there are plenty of unsolved questions. All three men continued taking their existing antiseizure medications throughout the trial, making it difficult to isolate the treatment’s effects. For example, could clozapine have somehow synergized with those medications to reduce seizure counts? The study was also open-label, without a placebo control. And clozapine, when taken at high doses, carries risks of heart and other problems , though the doses given here were much lower than those used in psychiatric disorders. Whether chemogenetics can deliver lasting seizure relief in larger groups remains to be seen. But its debut in human medicine is a hopeful glimpse of what’s possible, not just for epilepsy, but potentially for addiction, mood disorders, and other neurological conditions involving unbalanced brain circuits too. “These findings offer initial proof of concept,” the team wrote. The post Novel Gene Therapy Nearly Erases ‘Drug Resistant’ Seizures appeared first on SingularityHub .

items.descriptionOriginal: Wind turbines are designed to last for 20–25 years. By that measure, turbines around the world are an elderly lot. In the US alone, 7,500 wind turbines are at least 20 years old . As these clean energy-generating behemoths approach the end of their lives , their green reputation gets tainted. That’s because their large blades end up in landfills. Made to withstand the elements, turbine blades are so durable that breaking them down to recycle them is also not easy. But researchers at Tsinghua University have found a straightforward way to breathe new life into wind turbine blades. Their method turns old blades into two valuable manufacturing materials that can improve the mechanical and thermal properties of new blades. This new approach cuts greenhouse gas emissions by 83–92% compared to present-day recycling technique. The results can be found in the journal Chem Circularity . Wind turbine blades are made of tiny glass fibers in a resin that is made of chains that are linked closely. The fibers are difficult to separate from the resin for recycling. Existing recycling methods require rely on breaking down the resin with heat or chemical solvents. Besides consuming a lot of energy and producing chemical waste, these processes weaken the fibers and results in low-value materials. The Tsinghua team ground blade waste into powder and mixed it with carbon black. Then they place the mixture between electrodes and blast it with short intense pulses of electricity, using a technique called Flash Joule Heating. Therein lies a massive opportunity to decarbonize the grid. At these blistering temperatures, carbon reacts with silica to form silicon carbide, which is a tough, heat-resistant compound. Carbon atoms also reorganize into a one atom-thick lattice with a honeycomb structure, called graphene. Graphene, a material whose discoverers garnered the Nobel Prize, is known for its strength and ability to conduct heat and electricity. The process converted close to 60% of the mixture into a silicon carbide–graphene composite made up of 34% silicon carbide and 66% graphene. The researchers then added this composite to fresh epoxy resin for making new blades. Just 0.3% by weight of the additive made the new resin stiffer and stronger, which should increase lifetime of new blades. The researchers’ calculations also show that at commercial scale the new blade recycling approach could turn a profit of about $80 per ton of material because the recovered silicon carbide and graphene are valuable. Heat and chemical-based recycling methods, by comparison, cost $460 per ton and $1,800 per ton respectively, they say. “Many emerging waste streams, including aerospace composites, automotive lightweight structures, electronic encapsulants, and fiber-reinforced construction materials, share similar challenges,” the team writes in the paper. Their approach hints at a way to deal with those waste streams. The team is now working on ways to scale up their process. Source: Hao Bi et al. items.descriptionOriginal: This story was originally published by Grist . Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter here . Doing the laundry has grown easier and more efficient over the years, yet two things have always remained the same: A washing machine needs water, and a dryer needs heat. Technology designed to clean aerospace parts reimagines the process by ditching both of those in favor of an unlikely substitute: carbon dioxide, the very gas we’re trying so hard to contain. Under pressure, CO2 becomes a low-viscosity liquid capable of penetrating fabrics and carrying away oils and grime. When depressurized, it reverts to a gas, leaving clothes clean and dry. No wastewater. No dryer. Beyond its novelty, the idea could clean up a resource-intensive chore. The average family runs roughly 300 loads a year, consuming thousands of gallons of water. And more than 80 percent of U.S. households own a dryer, with one study putting the annual CO2 emissions from machine drying alone at 27 million metric tons . Tersus Solutions’ industrial CO2 washers use high pressure to turn carbon dioxide into a liquid that can clean fabrics without water. The machines’ bulky pressure chambers, pumps, pipes and compressors illustrate the challenge appliance makers face in trying to shrink the technology for household use. Courtesy of Teresus Solutions Long confined to industrial operations, liquid-CO2 cleaning is getting a second look from appliance giants LG and Samsung — this time for the home. Still, shrinking a technology built around bulky, high-pressure machinery to fit both a laundry room and household budget is a tall order. No less challenging is doing so without washing away the environmental gains that make waterless, dryerless laundry so enticing in the first place. Just getting this far has taken decades. Hughes Aircraft developed the process in 1990 to remove grease and other contaminants from electronic components. Electrolux later pursued it as a safer alternative to solvent-based dry cleaning, though cost, complexity, and bulky equipment kept it from catching on. In 2009, Colorado-based Tersus Solutions began refining the technology and has since carved out a niche cleaning outdoor apparel and equipment, as well as firefighter gear contaminated with hazardous residues. Its machines offer a glimpse of what CO2 cleaning can do and why squeezing it into a household appliance is no simple feat. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Tersus CEO Peter Whitcomb describes the machines as “futuristic front-loading washers,” though the company’s two models dwarf those found in a typical laundromat. Each occupies a roughly 10-foot cube, with the larger unit handling up to 85 pounds of laundry, or a dozen sleeping bags. Behind a thick, submarine-like hatch, a rotating drum sits inside a pressurized chamber amid a maze of pipes, pumps and compressors. Despite the complexity, what happens inside is relatively simple. Carbon dioxide turns from gas to liquid at 900 pounds per square inch of pressure — roughly one-third of what’s inside a full scuba tank . As it circulates, filters trap the grime, which accumulates as a thick purplish sludge for disposal. When the 45-minute cycle ends, the pressure drops and liquid returns to gas, instantly drying the load. More than 90 percent of the CO2 is recaptured for the next run; the rest escapes in a smoky wisp. The process is particularly effective on firefighter gear, with tests showing an average of more than 95 percent removal of contaminants such as PAHs, potentially harmful compounds found in smoke and soot. Water-soluble stains from sweat and food can be trickier, said Chris Robbins, Tersus’ chief technology officer, occasionally requiring pretreatment — “think Tide pen, but for CO2” — or conventional washing. For most loads, however, the process eliminates water and additives alike. “We’re not using detergent, we don’t use heat,” Whitcomb said. Tersus estimates its larger machines save roughly 300 gallons of water per load compared with conventional washing. There is another potential upside, as well: By eliminating wastewater and trapping shed fibers for disposal, the process could further reduce microplastic contamination from laundry. The energy equation, however, is more complicated. A California Energy Commission demonstration with the U.S. Navy found the method used about 15 percent less energy than smaller commercial washers and dryers, yet about as much as larger industrial combinations. Tersus has found comparable performance, said Robbins. While CO2 cleaning avoids thermal drying — typically the most energy-intensive part of conventional laundry — removing impurities from the carbon dioxide for reuse requires significant power. The company is exploring more efficient ways of heating and cooling the gas, Robbins said. As for the CO2, Tersus gets it from a nearby ethanol plant, where it’s a byproduct of fermentation. That minimizes transportation needs, although purifying and liquefying it require additional energy — further complicating the calculation of the technology’s overall carbon footprint. Then there’s the question of scale: Could all that machinery — enough to fill a small bedroom — be shrunk into a household appliance? LG and Samsung are working on that. Recent patents from the companies, both of which declined to comment, tackle distinct challenges: removing stains resistant to CO2 cleaning and reducing the pressure required to make the tech work. LG’s design uses detergents and other additives to help remove water-soluble stains. Although the patent doesn’t specify a formula, a recent study found that adding isopropyl alcohol and water improved liquid carbon dioxide’s ability to remove sugars, salts and other compounds. Samsung, meanwhile, proposes combining CO2 with other solvents to bring operating pressures down to a fraction of those used in industrial machines. That could make home models more compact, though some of the mixtures include PFAS , raising questions about environmental trade-offs. Smaller, however, doesn’t necessarily mean simpler. Separating and recovering those added solvents could require still more equipment, said Eckhard Groll, head of mechanical engineering at Purdue University and an expert in CO2 refrigeration. “There’s no question” that a home version is technically feasible, he said, “but it may be very costly, the technology.” Even if the machines become affordable, the environmental benefits may not carry over, said Rainer Stamminger, a household appliance efficiency researcher at the University of Bonn. With households running just a few loads a week, pressurizing and recovering carbon dioxide could be “very inefficient just for one wash” compared to industrial machines that run continuously. The economics may be especially challenging in the U.S., where electricity is relatively cheap. Groll pointed to heat pump dryers, which use about half the energy of conventional electric models. Popular in Europe, they made up 75 percent of new dryer sales in 2020, helped by higher electricity prices that helped ease the sticker shock; meanwhile, American sales still lag . CO2 washers could as well if their efficiency comes with a hefty upfront premium. Whitcomb sees greater opportunities in commercial dry cleaning, apartment buildings and institutions, where higher volumes could justify the equipment costs — and keep the machines running often enough to take advantage of their scale. With a new facility in Calgary expanding its Colorado operations, Tersus now works with more than 40 brands and retailers, offering repairs, restoration and resale services that “complement the cleaning” to extend garment life and keep products in circulation, Whitcomb said. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Even if engineers can make a home CO2 washer affordable and efficient, they would still have to convince people to buy one. The early market for water-efficient front-load washers offers a precedent: Energy and water savings attracted some consumers, while upfront costs deterred others. Performance and convenience mattered, too, said Gwendolyn Hustvedt, a textiles and consumer sciences professor at Texas State University who studied the trend. The technology may have one big selling point, however: The clothes come out dry. Beyond saving time and hassle, skipping what Hustvedt called “cooking your clothes in a box” could help garments last longer by reducing shrinkage and wear from heat and tumbling. Whether consumers would pay a premium for those benefits is another question. Home CO2 washers still have a long way to go before they break up the familiar washer-dryer combo. But if engineers can make the physics work economically — and environmentally — at household scale, the next big thing in laundry might be one less appliance. This article originally appeared in Grist at https://grist.org/science/carbon-dioxide-is-a-climate-problem-it-might-also-be-a-laundry-solution/ . Grist is a nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to reporting on climate change. items.descriptionOriginal: Garry oak trees, home for bluebirds nested in cavities, were tended by First Nations for millennia. Without their care, 95 percent of the Garry oak ecosystem was lost to agriculture, pesticides, and urban development. Their homes gone, bluebirds left, and were declared extinct on Vancouver Island and the southern Gulf Islands. “Garry oak trees are a great source of insects,” said Jacquie Taylor, coordinator for the Cowichan Bring Back the Bluebirds Project. “They have a real biodiversity of their own, things that live in the bark and on the trees.” Saving them would help save the bluebirds. Canadians and Americans worked together, along with a military base, a slew of permits, thousands of volunteer hours, private property owners, Cowichan Tribes, and lots and lots of tiny, wriggling mealworms to help the bluebirds return. “But most noticeable is the sound: a gentle musical chortling so cheerful and soothing that it immediately banishes all thought of the ills of the world.”

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Concentrations of PFOS and PFOA, the two most toxic forever chemicals , have fallen by 30 percent and 29 percent in England’s rivers over the past 10 years, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA). In freshwater fish , levels are down 49 percent. The agency attributes the decline to restrictions that removed both compounds from most products, which makes the data one of the clearer measures yet of what a chemical ban does to a river system over time. Two forever chemicals, two bans, one decade of data PFOS and PFOA PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, were first developed in the U.S. in the 1930s. Manufacturers adopted them for their resistance to oil, water, and heat, and they ended up in nonstick pans, firefighting foam, and electrical components. The same chemical stability means they take a very long time to break down, which earned them the label forever chemicals. PFOS and PFOA were among the earliest compounds in the family. About 20 years ago, researchers began linking them to tissue damage in animals and to higher rates of certain serious illnesses in people, including testicular cancer . The UK all but banned PFOS in 2010 and PFOA in 2020. Results from the latest Environment Agency figures The new data, published by the EA this month, covers 10 years of monitoring. Both chemicals declined by nearly a third in river water, while the near-halving in fish points to less of the compounds moving up the food chain. Dr. David Megson, a reader in environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University, welcomed the trend. “It’s brilliant to see how far we have come in the last 10 years,” he said. Lower concentrations, same total load Where forever chemicals go after a ban The EA report attaches a significant caveat to its own numbers. Because PFOS and PFOA break down so slowly, the total quantity in the environment has likely not changed much. Concentrations in rivers have dropped because the chemicals have been diluted and carried downstream into the sea. A ban stops new inputs, but it does not remove what is already circulating. Very few methods can destroy PFAS permanently. High-temperature incineration is one of them, and England currently has only two facilities suited to the job. Making polluters pay Megson sees the monitoring record as a starting point for accountability. “There is a lot to do, and this report provides an essential foundation to support investigations to make the polluters pay for any damage they have caused,” he said. Regulating PFAS as a group 15,000 compounds, 200 in common use PFOS and PFOA are two of an estimated 15,000 PFAS, of which around 200 are in frequent use. The EA said that “uncertainty remains regarding the toxicity of many PFAS” and that its findings reinforce the case for regulating the chemicals as a class instead of one at a time. The chemicals industry has long resisted a group approach, arguing that evidence of toxicity for most other PFAS is limited or absent and that some have essential applications, including in life-saving medical equipment. Wider monitoring The agency now tests regularly for 60 additional PFAS to map contamination across England, and the government announced earlier this month that it will begin measuring forever chemicals in people’s bodies. Taken together with the river data, those programs will show whether the pattern seen with PFOS and PFOA holds for other compounds once restrictions arrive: a slow but steady fall in water and wildlife, with the legacy load still to be dealt with downstream. items.title: Οι οικολόγοι ακολούθησαν ένα ίχνος βελανιδιών. Οδήγησε στη νόσο του Lyme.
items.titleOriginal: Ecologists followed an acorn trail. It led to Lyme disease.
items.description: Όταν οι άνθρωποι επινόησαν την παροιμία ότι «οι πανίσχυρες βελανιδιές από μικρά βελανίδια φυτρώνουν», σίγουρα δεν σκέφτονταν τη νόσο του Lyme. Αλλά τα κυριολεκτικά βελανίδια -όχι ποιητικές μεταφορές- αποδεικνύεται ότι παίζουν έναν εκπληκτικά μεγάλο ρόλο στην εξάπλωση αυτής της πανίσχυρης ασθένειας που μεταδίδεται από κρότωνες, σύμφωνα με μια πρόσφατη δημοσίευση στο Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Ένα κύμα μέσα…
items.descriptionOriginal: When people coined the proverb that “mighty oaks from little acorns grow”, they certainly weren’t thinking of Lyme disease. But literal acorns—not poetic metaphors—turn out to play a surprisingly big role in the spread of this mighty tick-borne illness, according to a recent paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences . A surge in acorns one year can translate into a boom two years later in the population of ticks that transmit the disease to people. This discovery illustrates the ways in which a web of tiny, interconnected things—acorns, mice, microbes—can have big and unexpected consequences for people. It also shows that it can take decades of scientific research to decipher the head-scratching complexity of ecosystems. The results are “helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk,” said Shannon LaDeau, one of the paper’s authors and an ecologist with the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in New York State’s Hudson River Valley. LaDeau and colleague Richard Ostfeld oversee a Lyme-related research program at the institute that stretches back more than 30 years, just a few decades after the disease was first identified. Over that time, scientists have turned plots of New York forestland into an outdoor Lyme laboratory. They’ve assembled mountains of data tracking the ups and downs of a huge range of elements: temperature, rainfall, oak seedlings, mouse populations, tick numbers, infection rates, you name it. The results have repeatedly surprised scientists, defying expectations about the disease. It’s been known since the 1980s that the disease is caused by the bacteria Borrelia burgdorferi. The bite of an infected deer tick transmits the bacterium to people, causing flu-like symptoms that can escalate to chronic fatigue, memory loss, depression and even brain swelling and cardiac problems. More than 450,000 cases are reported in the U.S. each year, plus more than 200,000 in Europe. Despite the tick’s association with deer, the Cary Institute work didn’t bear out initial suspicions that more white-tailed deer translated into more dangers for people. The researchers found no correlation between deer numbers and the abundance of tick nymphs—the life stage when they most commonly transmit the disease to people. Nor did they find a link to seasonal temperature extremes. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {height: auto;position: relative;}.IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby:hover , Lyme Disease: Prescribed fire Instead, the researchers uncovered evidence of a cascade of cause and effect between oak trees, white-footed mice and ticks. Acorns from red oak trees at the study sites are a primary food source for the mice. The year after a big acorn harvest, the mouse population boomed, the scientists found. The mice, in turn, are a prime feeding target for larval ticks which go on to become nymphs the following year. A big year for mice translated into a roughly 40% increase in abundance of tick nymphs the next year. All this thanks to a bumper crop in acorns two years earlier. While acorns aren’t abundant everywhere that the disease occurs, fluctuations in other crucial mouse food, such as seeds, could have the same effect, the scientists wrote. While it took years to tease apart these dynamics, researchers were still puzzled by other patterns. A surge in mice meant more ticks—and therefore a greater risk of people getting infected. But it didn’t translate into a higher percentage of the ticks themselves carrying the disease, the data showed. “It kept me up at night,” Ostfeld said of the result. “It meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong.” An apparent answer emerged when the researchers looked not just at the mouse population, but at a variety of small mammals. The long-term study plots were located in relatively intact forest that supported a range of other warm-blooded critters, such as skunks, squirrels and opossums. Many of these creatures are less prone to getting infected when a tick feeds on them, which also means they are less likely to spread the bacteria to other ticks. As a consequence, the percentage of infected ticks was driven not just by the number of mice but the population of a range of creatures. By contrast, in nearby places where forests had been broken into pieces by human intrusion , the diversity of small mammals was smaller. In those spots, where ticks had fewer options, higher mouse numbers did translate into more infected ticks. So in addition to small things like acorns, add two very big things that shape people’s risk of encountering Lyme disease: loss of habitat and of biodiversity.
